title: How has AI and tech changed your life? Australians share their stories
text:
Technology is creeping into every facet of our lives, for better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder, but it is certainly here to stay.

Australians are grappling with the prospects of AI replacing jobs, privacy breaches, misinformation and digital exclusion, while also benefiting from technology designed to make everyday tasks easier.

We want to hear your stories and experiences in our live blog below, where you can also put your questions to cybersecurity expert Mihai Lazarescu from Curtin University and the ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson.

title: Runner smashes half-marathon record, heads straight to the football
text:
Yomif Kejelcha has smashed the half-marathon world record, running a staggering 56 minutes and 51 seconds at the Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires in Argentina on Sunday.

The Ethiopian shaved 29 seconds off the previous mark of 57:20, which had been set by Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in Lisbon in March.

Kejelcha's time and that of the record he just beat are still subject to ratification by World Athletics.

The Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires is a World Athletics Label road race and took place under favourable conditions of 6 degrees Celsius and with a slight breeze.

As ever, the super shoe gets plenty of post-race love from Yomif Kejelcha. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Tadese Worku (59:20) and Bereket Nega (1:00:20) of Ethiopia completed the podium.

"I'm over the moon," Kejelcha told World Athletics.

"I'm super happy and right now I don't feel any tiredness. The travel from Ethiopia was too long and I was tired the first days here, but later I felt better and today I was full of beans.

"I had planned to run conservatively over the early stages, but I felt good and decided to give it my all.

"This time is unbelievable. I can't describe it with words.

"I now hope to try the Argentinian meat, which has a very good reputation, and this afternoon I have been invited to watch the River Plate-Vélez football match. I'm very grateful."

At the historic Estadio Monumental, Kejelcha showed off his new record on a new River Plate shirt, although would have been disappointed as Vélez Sarsfield came from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 in their Argentine Primera División clash. Clearly Los Millonarios don't share Kejelcha's stamina.

Yomif Kejelcha showed off his record on a new River Plate kit at at the Estadio Monumental. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Kejelcha's time allowed him to reclaim the record, which he previously held with a 57:30 in Valencia in October 2024.

The time is slower than that recorded by Kiplimo in Barcelona last year, when he ran what he described as "the perfect race" to stop the clock in 56:42.

But World Athletics did not ratify that time because race conditions did not comply with their regulations.

Kejelcha ran the race at an average pace of 2 minutes and 42 seconds per kilometre — which would give you a 5km parkrun time of 13 minutes and 28 seconds.

However, as was the case when he became the second man to run an official race marathon in less than two hours in London last year, he negative split the race, running the second half faster than the first.

Super shoes won't be banned despite 'technological doping' claims Lord Sebastian Coe says World Athletics has a duty to "enable" super shoe development despite concerns.

He set out behind two pacemakers, going through the first 5km at 13:45, while the second 5km was run in 13:34.

His subsequent 5km split was a remarkable 13:22, with the Ethiopian holding that pace through the next 5km, running it in 13:23.

Last April at the London Marathon, the 29-year-old two-time Olympian ran 1:59:41, finishing second behind Kenya's Sabastian Sawe, who set the world record with a 1:59:30.

In the women's race, Ethiopia's Fotyen Tesfay stormed to victory in 1:03:57, comfortably beating her two Kenyan rivals Nelvin Jepkemboi (1:05:06) and Catherine Amanang'ole (1:05:11).

title: National rental prices rise to half average Australian income
text:
The average apartment now costs half of the average Australian income to rent, with prices exceeding the 30 per cent housing stress mark even for six-figure earners, according to a new report.

Housing advocacy group Everybody's Home has found renting a unit now costs more than half the median take-home pay of a single worker in every Australian capital city.

The 2026 Priced Out report found apartments on average nationally cost $614 per week, making up 56 per cent of the take-home income of someone earning $70,000 — close to Australia's median income of $74,100.

Everybody’s Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said this was a "crisis that continues to get worse for the country's renters".

"We now see people earning really high incomes are still spending more than a third of their income on rent. If you are earning $130,000 a year, you are still spending more than a third on rent," she said.

"If you are earning an average income between $70,000 and $80,000 and living in a capital city, you are spending two-thirds of your income to afford the average rent.

" We are seeing across the board renters can't avoid rental stress anywhere in the country, which is dire. "

The report found northern WA, the Gold Coast and Sydney were the three most expensive places to rent, followed by the Sunshine Coast and Perth.

"For a long time Sydney was ground zero for the crisis and it is still really bad news, shocking if you are a renter in Sydney," Ms Azize said.

"This year one of the most expensive – the most expensive capital city in the country is Perth and WA across the board has some really dire results.

"The Gold Coast has been surging every year that we have done this report and it is getting expensive to rent on the Gold Coast, even if you are earning $130,000 a year, you can't afford to rent on the Gold Coast. You would need to be in a couple or a multi-income family to make that work."

The report found, for someone earning $70,000, median Sydney rent would take 69 per cent of their weekly pay, while even Adelaide — the cheapest capital — would cost more than half.

Changes and recommendations

Changes to housing policy in this year's budget were predicted by the government to result in a median rental increase of $2 a week.

However, Ms Azize said rents had been surging by about 10 per cent every single year.

"I think it's a bit of an insult to people's intelligence when the industry comes out and says that any rent increases from here are going to be down to these changes," she said.

"Any renter in Australia knows that they get whacked with a huge rent increase every single year."

However, she said changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were positive overall.

"They're changes that we've been pushing for a really long time," she said.

"They're really good news for anyone who wants to make the housing system fairer, especially those renters who are trying to save to buy.

"But what these results show us is that the federal government and state and territory governments especially now really need to turn their attention to renters and taking some steps to limit rent increases because there's really only so much that people can afford to pay."

Rental prices have been surging over the past few years. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The report recommends several recommendations, including the Australian government committing to build 940,000 public and community homes over the next 15 years; introducing limits on the number and amount of rent increases during a tenancy and ending no-grounds evictions.

"For the past four decades we've seen the federal government especially really step back from funding housing, from playing a role, and they're leaving it entirely to the private sector," Ms Azize said.

"We can see that over that same period renting has become incredibly expensive.

"So we need to see the government step back in.

"When you look around the world at the countries that are actually doing a good job of turning around their housing crisis or better yet avoiding it altogether, they're the countries where the government is playing a really big role in providing housing. They're not just leaving it to the private sector."

title: KPMG to cut almost 400 jobs after audit leaks scandal
text:
Accounting firm KPMG says it will cut 27 partners and about 360 staff from its local arm, and revamp its structure as it grapples with lower revenue from lost contracts following the audit leaks scandal.

The company's revenue fell from $2.28 billion the previous year, to $2.26 billion in the 2026 financial year, and KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams expected more revenue falls.

KPMG has been unable to retain most of its ongoing government contracts after allegations KPMG audit partners misused client data and then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it.

In March, Labor senator Deborah O'Neill shared with parliament a whistleblower's allegations that confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus.

And earlier this month, the firm's current and former partners were hauled before a federal inquiry probing why the firm allegedly shared client information and ignored the whistleblower's allegations when they first surfaced.

Five former KPMG partners were grilled in camera: Julian McPherson (left), Kim Lawry, Martin Sheppard, Andrew Yates and Eileen Hoggett. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The job cuts at KPMG's Australian arm were widely expected as the firm reportedly sought financial support from KPMG International to remain solvent.

PwC review doesn't stop conflicts of interest Former Telstra chief Ziggy Switkowski has unveiled a review of PwC, but it's unlikely this is the end of an intense probe of its business and the way other consulting firms manage conflicts of interest.

KPMG is one of the "big four" accounting firms, which have taken a hit to their bottom line from getting fewer ongoing government consulting contracts, following the earlier tax leaks controversy at PricewaterhouseCoopers.

Mr Sams said in a statement the firm was cutting 5 per cent of its workforce, primarily in its consulting arm, "in response to continued economic weakness, difficult market conditions and the impact of the firm's conduct and whistleblower matters".

This includes 27 partners and about 360 employees.

"This is not a decision that has been taken lightly, and we know it will have a very real impact on people," Mr Sams said.

With demand for consulting remaining weaker, "most of the roles affected will be in our consulting business".

"Changes to our business and the professional services landscape have also reduced the need for some roles in business services," he said.

"Our immediate focus is on treating everyone impacted with care, dignity and respect. We are providing practical support and making wellbeing support central to the process."

More job cuts could follow

The company will also restructure so that the firm's mid-market and private deals team joins deal advisory and infrastructure, while its advisory team joins consulting.

Accounting firms could be split post KPMG scandal Accounting firms could be asked to split their lucrative consulting services from their audit functions, under a shake up of the industry being consulted on by the federal government.

These changes would align KPMG Australia more closely with its global advisory services.

The firm would also begin consultation on "a small number of award-based roles".

Mr Sams said more cuts could follow.

"The changes announced today are an important step in the longer work of renewing and rebuilding our firm," he said.

The firm was undertaking "internal and external reviews" in the wake of the whistleblower's allegations, which he said "will be completed in the coming months".

"Their findings will inform the next phase of our action plan and help ensure we take all necessary action," he said.

KPMG has faced months of scrutiny over its handling of a whistleblower complaint. (ABC)

Mr Sams thanked the firm's staff after a "very challenging year".

"They [KPMG employees] continued to deliver outstanding work for more than 13,000 clients, while supporting one another through a difficult period for the firm," he said.

" Our total revenue was slightly lower than last year, and below our expectations. "

Consulting takes a hit, audit and tax divisions grow

While consulting took a hit, revenue grew in four out of five divisions, led by audit and assurance, up 11 per cent, and tax and legal, up 10.9 per cent.

"We also continued to invest significantly in technology and build our AI capability, helping our people work more effectively and deliver better outcomes for clients."

But the firm needed to "be clear about the outlook".

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

"We expect difficult market conditions to continue in FY27 and beyond," Mr Sams said.

"Economic growth is expected to remain subdued until at least 2028, affecting client investment and extending decision-making timeframes," he said.

"The professional services sector is also changing rapidly as client expectations evolve, AI reshapes the way services are delivered, and government spending on consultants remains lower.

"We also recognise the challenges created by our own failings, and the work we must continue to do to rebuild trust.

"While these conditions are likely to persist, we remain focused on what we can control. We will continue to monitor performance closely, act when needed and consider carefully how the firm needs to be set up for the future."

title: Racehorse injury rules under spotlight after jockey's death
text:
A coroner has recommended more stringent reporting standards for racehorses returning from injury after the death of a French apprentice jockey in the New South Wales Central West more than four years ago.

Marina Morel died during track work at Gulgong Racecourse on February 8, 2022.

The 30-year-old was riding Lina's Choice when the mare suffered a catastrophic leg injury while galloping past the winning post.

Morel was thrown to the ground before Lina's Choice rolled on top of her, causing blunt-force injuries to her head, neck and chest.

Morel was flown to Westmead Hospital in Sydney, where she died four days later.

Lina's Choice was euthanased at the racecourse.

An inquest into Morel's death examined whether a previous injury suffered by Lina's Choice contributed to the fall, and whether the jockey's death could have been prevented.

Marina Morel started as an apprentice jockey at the Gulgong Turf Club in 2021. (ABC News)

Horse appropriately managed, coroner finds

Morel came to Australia from France in 2014 to pursue her ambition of becoming a professional jockey and was working for Gulgong trainer Brett Thompson at BKB Racing at the time of the incident.

Lina's Choice suffered a ligament injury to her right front leg in March 2021.

Veterinarian Jack Holman recommended Lina's Choice rest for nine to 12 months but the mare returned to work after six months and 22 days.

Despite the earlier return, Deputy State Coroner Derek Lee found the rest period was consistent with academic literature for similar injuries and that Thompson appropriately managed the mare's return to work.

"Mr Thompson followed his usual practice for the management of horses returning to work from injury for Lina's Choice, which was appropriate," he said.

Brett Thompson has been a professional trainer for more than 15 years. (Supplied: Brett Thompson Racing)

Judge Lee also found there were no signs of lameness during the mare's recovery and no evidence that the way she returned to training or racing predisposed her to stress fractures.

He said evidence suggested the mare was also performing "well above expectations" in the lead-up to the fatal fall.

After returning to work, Lina's Choice participated in a barrier trial and two races at Wellington and Dubbo before Ms Morel's death.

Six days before the fatal incident, equine chiropractor Gary Christou detected some chest stiffness, and recommended Lina's Choice be monitored.

Judge Lee found that response was appropriate and that the stiffness alone did not indicate a veterinary assessment was required.

The coroner found Lina's Choice had nevertheless developed stress fractures in her left humerus, which resulted in the catastrophic fracture during track work.

"There is no evidence that the previous injury was associated with the stress fractures," Judge Lee said.

Marina Morel trained as a jockey in Sydney and Mudgee. (Supplied)

Calls for stronger safeguards

Judge Lee made several recommendations aimed at strengthening Racing NSW's oversight of horses returning from injury or extended breaks from training and racing.

He recommended Racing NSW develop and publish clearer guidance about what constituted a "major orthopaedic injury" that took into account the nature and extent of an injury, the treatment required and how long a horse was unable or not recommended to train or race.

Judge Lee also called for broader reporting requirements for trainers, including matters that could affect a horse's performance even where it appeared to have recovered before being nominated for a race.

Racing NSW requires horses that have not raced or trialled for 150 days or more to undergo an official veterinary examination and barrier trial before returning to racing.

Judge Lee called for that requirement to be formalised in a published policy and for Racing NSW to explore whether the 150-day threshold could be reduced, potentially to 60 days.

Morel's family attended the hearing remotely from France and had the assistance of an interpreter. Her mother wiped tears from her eyes at the conclusion of the hearing.

title: 'Disappointed' Hird congratulates McVeigh ahead of Bombers coach call
text:
Mark McVeigh appears set to be unveiled as Essendon's next senior coach, with fellow applicant James Hird congratulating his former teammate on the impending appointment.

Bombers legend Hird had been vocal in expressing his desire to return for another stint as coach, after Brad Scott was sacked in May.

Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide assistant Murray Davis were also in the mix.

But McVeigh, an assistant to Dean Cox at Sydney, is reportedly on the verge of being appointed, with an announcement expected as soon as tomorrow.

Mark McVeigh is in the box seat to be offered the Bombers job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Interim coach Dean Solomon hands over the reins after the Bombers (2-21) completed the worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

"Firstly, congratulations to Mark. He's a great friend of mine and I'm very proud of him that he's going to be named the coach, so good on him," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

"From a personal point of view, it's very disappointing. I'm disappointed. I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes."

Hird indicated he was yet to hear an official decision from Essendon, but said "maybe that's coming".

The 53-year-old ruled out returning to the Bombers in a different role, but said he still had the passion to coach.

James Hird, Dean Solomon and Mark McVeigh together in 2022 when they were all at the Giants. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Hird is director of coaching with VFL club Port Melbourne.

"We have a finals series to play," Hird said.

"We'll see what plays out at the end of the year with some other clubs who have contacted me and we'll see what happens."

McVeigh is reportedly set to present to the Essendon board again today, with an announcement imminent.

The 45-year-old played 232 games for Essendon and was one of the 34 players suspended over the club's devastating drugs saga, when Hird was coach.

McVeigh currently serves as Sydney's defensive coach, but could leave the club immediately to play a role in the Bombers' end-of-season exit meetings and list management decisions.

The second-placed Swans are preparing for a finals campaign while bracing for more fallout from the scandal that has rocked the club.

"That's one thing this football club's done well for a long period of time … be ready for the unexpected or if something does arise," Sydney coach Cox said last week about the potential of losing McVeigh to the Bombers.

"We've had those meetings [and] discussions. We're really clear on what will happen if he was or wasn't to get the [Essendon] position."

Two-time Essendon premiership champion and former captain Hird first took over as Bombers coach in 2010.

He was suspended for the 2014 season amid the fallout from the drugs saga, returned as coach in 2015 and resigned in August that year.

Hird had garnered plenty of support from Bombers fans in his latest bid to return as coach, after he narrowly missed out when Scott was appointed in 2022.

title: Sugarcane farmers question APVMA paraquat ban
text:
Cane growers say a decision by the chemical regulator to ban them using controversial herbicide paraquat could lead to worse outcomes for the environment while they search for an alternative.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) released its review of paraquat and diquat in June, which significantly reduced the application rates allowed in most broadacre crops.

Chemical regulator approves paraquat use The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority concludes its nearly 30-year review of the controversial but popular herbicide.

But sugarcane growers were given two years to phase out its use completely before the chemical would no longer be registered for use on their crop.

The APVMA said the review assessed each paraquat use pattern separately against current environmental safety standards and found an unacceptable risk to birds foraging in cane growing areas.

But Canegrowers chief executive Dan Galligan said growers feared the move could lead to worse environmental outcomes than those the regulator was trying to prevent.

"The lack of alternatives means there's a lot of stress and concern," he said.

" What it means is usually changing farming systems to something that's more expensive or sometimes even worse in terms of environmental outcomes. "

Bird health concerns

Paraquat is used early in the planting of the crop because it kills weeds quickly but does not linger in the soil, allowing the young cane to get established.

Mr Galligan said Sugar Research Australia was looking at suitable alternatives, but there was no timeline on when that would be delivered.

Dan Galligan is concerned about what the APVMA's decision will mean for sugarcane farmers. (Supplied: Canegrowers)

In the interim, he said changes to the farming system to achieve the same results would be "dramatic".

"Effectively, we're going to have to use more herbicides and possibly increase our sediment loss on farms, which is not really what we want to try and do," he said.

The APVMA acknowledged growers may need to change weed management practices, but said alternatives and the economic impacts of those changes were matters for growers, advisers, industry and state governments to manage.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the regulator said the use pattern in sugarcane posed acute and chronic exposure risks to birds foraging in treated areas.

"The supported sugarcane use patterns did not meet the required environmental safety standards," it said.

"Therefore [those use patterns] were not retained on approved labels," a spokesperson for the regulator said.

Adrian Crema grows sugarcane and bananas near Tully in Far North Queensland. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

But growers in Far North Queensland dispute the conclusion.

Tully farmer Bryce MacDonald said the APVMA's decision was "bizarre".

"I've never seen any bird die from paraquat," he said.

"In fact, I reckon there's more birds around than there ever was, and some other people have voiced that to me as well."

Nearby sugarcane and banana farmer Adrian Crema said growers did not understand why the risks could not be managed.

"I personally have never seen a dead bird as a result of spraying paraquat in a cane paddock," he said.

Without paraquat, the sugarcane industry will need to make changes. (ABC News: Yasmine Wright Gittins)

Growers using paraquat are able to adopt a minimal till farming system, which means they disturb the soil less and reduce run-off to the Great Barrier Reef.

"How are we going to grow sugarcane without paraquat?" Mr Crema said.

"Do they want us to go back to cultivating … to use more heavy residual chemicals which are more toxic to fish?

"There are a lot of confused cane farmers out there right now who want answers."

Approved uses

Paraquat has previously been linked to an increased risk of Parkinson's disease, although the APVMA's review found the evidence did not support a link between exposure through approved uses and the disease.

There is no timeline for when an alternative to paraquat for sugarcane will be available. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Australia's peak body for Parkinson's disease disputes that finding.

Neurologists say warnings met with silence by chemical watchdog Dozens of neurologists are concerned "real world" human studies linking paraquat to Parkinson's disease are being overlooked as the regulator weighs up the future of the controversial weed killer.

Under the new restrictions, sugarcane farmers are still able to use paraquat on farm for fallow crops, headlands and fire breaks in the same paddock, but not on the sugarcane crop itself.

Mr MacDonald said that only added to the confusion and farmers should be trusted to use the product by the label.

"Farmers don't waste money. They don't waste chemicals. They use them conservatively," he said.

The APVMA said it did not assess crops based solely on where they were grown, and therefore different crops could receive different regulatory outcomes even when they were grown in similar regions.

title: Former Roosters premiership star unveiled as PNG Chiefs' '007' signing
text:
Joey Manu has been unveiled as the much-hyped PNG Chief 007, with the two-time premiership winner to return to the NRL in 2028.

The Chiefs officially confirmed today the former Sydney Roosters utility signed a two-year deal with the club, which now boasts a backline that will be the envy of the NRL.

PNG had long hyped their seventh signing, with speculation Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary was bound for the club as their inaugural halfback.

But with a staircase at their home base showing each of their signings and "007" listed as "reserved", that honour will now go to code-hopper Manu ahead of the 2028 season.

Loading Instagram content

"We're thrilled to add Joey to our squad moving forward," Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas said.

"He is a world-class footballer with versatility across several positions and can change a game in a single moment with the skills he possesses.

"His experience and demonstrated success at the highest level will be a great benefit to our team and we can't wait to see him have a significant impact in the Chiefs jersey."

Manu joins a list that already includes Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Zac Lomax, Brian To'o and Englishman Matty Lees.

But the move appears likely to have ended the 30-year-old's boyhood dream of representing the All Blacks.

To'o is still just the beginning for PNG Brian To'o is the fourth player to sign for Papua New Guinea who has played State of Origin in the past two years. It's a sign of things to come, with the NRL's richest club yet to truly enter free agency.

Manu left the NRL for an overseas rugby union career after the 2024 season, starting in Japan before a move to French team Racing 92 last year.

But his French rugby deal runs to the end of 2027, and New Zealand Rugby only selects players for the All Blacks if they play domestically.

Manu will be 33 by the time his Chiefs deal finishes.

Manu became one of the NRL's most prized utility players across 181 games, including the 2018 and 2019 premiership wins, with the Roosters.

He was named Dally M centre of the year in 2022 and won the Golden Boot award as the sport's best international player later that year.

The athletic New Zealand representative is equally adept in the centres and at fullback, and can also capably slot into the halves in a pinch.

On leaving the NRL after the Roosters' 2024 finals campaign, Manu offered no guarantees of ever returning to the 13-man code.

But any possible comeback had widely been expected to come with the Roosters, who scouted him as a teenager.

Instead, Manu becomes the latest jewel in the crown of the NRL's forthcoming 19th team, which can offer lucrative tax-free salaries to its signings.

PNG will be able to officially hit the market on November 1, with Cleary headlining a list of players who could still become free agents at that time.

The club has also been linked to Gold Coast utility AJ Brimson and Canberra second-rower Hudson Young, both of whom are State of Origin players, in recent weeks.

Isaah Yeo, Latrell Mitchell and Bradman Best are among other household names without deals beyond the 2027 season.

title: Once Australia's northern capital, Newcastle Waters became a ghost town
text:
In an abandoned hotel in the Northern Territory ghost town of Newcastle Waters, Wayne Kraft says he can hear the walls talk.

Walking through the building, he imagines the patrons and staff once occupying what was the only pub for hundreds of kilometres in every direction.

"It's the pub with no beer," he says from the front bar, a stubby from home in hand.

"It just reeks of that history."

Today, Newcastle Waters is a humble collection of deserted buildings and tin sheds, but imagine an alternate reality where the town is not only alive, but thriving as the capital of North Australia.

A century ago, a plan was hatched to bring this idea to life.

How did this community rise to have the status of a capital city, before entering terminal decline?

Before: Newcastle Waters in 1978 after the town was abandoned. (Supplied: Library and Archives NT) . . After: People gather in Newcastle Waters in 2026. (ABC News) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Newcastle Waters in 1978 after the town was abandoned. (Supplied: Library and Archives NT) / People gather in Newcastle Waters in 2026. (ABC News)

Stockmen and drovers

In 1926, the NT was still governed by the federal government in Canberra, which felt the best way to run its most far-flung jurisdiction was to split it in two.

Alice Springs would be the capital of Central Australia, and Newcastle Waters would take the crown off Darwin and become the new capital of the north.

This made sense for two reasons, according to Mr Kraft, an amateur historian from Alice Springs.

There was no road access to Darwin, and the city was generally accessed by sea.

And Newcastle Waters was already a hive of activity, due to the famous Overland Telegraph Line located nearby and the stock routes that converged on the settlement.

"I've walked in here on my own, and I can hear the walls talk; go into the kitchen and just visualise people, the ladies cooking with their long gowns," says Mr Kraft, known as Krafty.

"There's big mobs of cattle moving through here. I can only visualise what it would have been like."

Stockmen at Newcastle Waters Station on Christmas Day 1931. (Supplied: Library and Archives NT)

The town was built on the edge of a cattle station of the same name, which still operates today. At its peak Newcastle Waters was a vital stop for drovers taking thousands of cattle from as far as Western Australia's Kimberley on a 1,500-kilometre journey to Queensland.

A small school remains for Aboriginal communities in the region, but there are no residents.

One of the most notorious routes was the Murranji Track, a treacherously remote 234-kilometre trip from Top Springs to Newcastle Waters. Some drovers called it the "death track", but it was the only way to move cattle before modern roads and trucks.

Jock Jones in his store at Newcastle Waters. It was a crucial supply point for drovers. (Supplied: Library and Archives NT)

Former drover Roger Steele was only a teenager when he first travelled the Murranji in 1956.

"We collected 1,350 wild bullocks. There was only six people in the camp, and we started moving them towards Queensland," he says.

"It took 16 weeks, and we had to get through the Murranji, so that's scary, all that scrub out there. And if the cattle rush [stampede], what are you going to do, for God's sake?"

Mr Steele later left the industry and was elected to the first NT parliament in 1974.

" I've been droving a heck of a lot, more than I really wanted to. I 'enjoyed' it so much, I got into parliament to get away from the cattle. "

Historian Eddie Webber (left) and Roger Steele (right) with a plaque listing the names of drovers known to have travelled the Murranji. (ABC Rural: Sam Parry)

Aboriginal stockmen were also essential to the industry's success. However, many were treated unfairly, and strikes were common across the region.

This included Newcastle Waters Station, where in 1966 dozens of Indigenous workers went on strike to demand equal pay, months before the now legendary Wave Hill walk-off.

The movement was also a call to recognise the injustices perpetrated by colonists, and the Wave Hill walk-off is widely considered to have inspired the Aboriginal Land Rights Act.

Horses inside a post and rail yard at Newcastle Waters in 1930. (Supplied: Library and Archives NT)

Mates of the Murranji

Preserving the history of Newcastle Waters is a passion for people like Mr Kraft. He has pulled a group of friends together to form Mates of the Murranji, a club dedicated to bringing new life, and hopefully tourists, to the ghost town.

"People can slowly [walk] around the township, absorb the history," he says.

" I just think it's a fantastic story, if you're at a quiz night and it came up, we could win the competition. "

Their cause has attracted interest in Darwin's corridors of power; the late Ted Egan, a renowned musician and statesman, was a mate of the Murranji. Recently a convoy of nearly 70 people travelled to Newcastle Waters to celebrate the centenary of its selection as capital.

Among them were long-time Territorians, such as Mr Steele, NT Administrator David Connolly and ministers in the NT government.

Mates of the Murranji out the front of Jock Jones's old store in Newcastle Waters. (ABC Rural: Sam Parry)

As for why the decision to make Newcastle Waters a capital city did not stick, Krafty has a simple explanation.

"Probably no money; decisions made in Canberra often don't resonate here in the Territory even to this day," he says.

"That actual act of parliament was rescinded five years later.

" Darwin always retained its position as the capital of the NT. "

By the end of the 60s, the NT's road network had improved drastically, and road trains became the preferred mode of transport for cattle.

The stock routes were no longer needed, and the town's fate was sealed.

But if Krafty has his way, Canberra's big dreams for Newcastle Waters could finally be realised, just a century later than planned.

title: Aussie athletes continue top form with trio of medals at Diamond League
text:
Commonwealth Games champions Eleanor Patterson and Rose Davies have kicked on from their Glasgow triumphs, along with double silver medallist Jessica Hull, as Australia's athletes have continued to shine on the Diamond League circuit in Poland.

All three made the podium at the Diamond League Silesia meet in Chorzów overnight, with high jump champion Patterson soaring to third place, Glasgow 5,000/10,000 metre double winner Davies grabbing bronze in the 5,000m and Hull running her fastest race of the year to finish 1,500m runner-up.

But there was disappointment for Glasgow sprint hero Lachlan Kennedy, who after his Australian-record run for silver at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium, failed to make the 100m final in Chorzów.

Pride of place went to Olympic silver medallist Hull, who tried out new tactics, sitting back in the field in the Silesian Stadium and kicking for home at the top of the straight, only to be reeled in by Ethiopia's Tsige Duguma. She needed a 2026 world-leading time of three minutes and 55.06 seconds to pip Hull's 3:55.20.

"I got caught in the last few metres but it was a big step forwards in confidence today," said Hull, who is eyeing the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest next month.

"That's the fastest I've run all year and we have some good races to come over the next few weeks."

Davies earned her second career Diamond League podium as she pursued Italian favourite Nadia Battocletti, fresh from her own 5,000/10,000 double at the European Championships.

Davies eventually finished third in 14:55.39, pipped by Ethiopia's Freweyni Hailu and Battocletti, who won in 14:54.09.

"Every race is a step forward and to come top three at a Diamond League shows I'm in good form," Davies said.

"I really look up to Battocletti, she's a great athlete and I would love to be like her."

Australia's Eleanor Patterson earned bronze during the women's high jump final. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Patterson again defeated teammate, world champion Nicola Olyslagers, just as she had done in Glasgow when they took gold and silver.

It was a strong effort considering Patterson was battling illness, but she had to settle for third behind Ukrainian rivals, Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh and Iryna Gerashchenko.

Kennedy took his first strides back on the international circuit after his historic 9.85sec silver medal-winning run in Glasgow, but his 10.08sec run in the heats in Chorzów was not enough to earn him a place in the final, which was later won by Jamaica's world champion, Oblique Seville, in a searing 9.83sec.

"I didn't come out as well as I would've liked but I'm just trying to shake the rust off a bit. I'll get back into some training and better form — I'm happy," Kennedy said.

Triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall cleared 5.90m but it only earned him fifth place while his mate Armand Duplantis earned yet another effortless triumph with a 6.20m winner.

Queensland's two-time Diamond League champion Matthew Denny finished eighth in the discus (66.38m), as Lithuania's world record holder Mykolas Alekna won with a competition record 72.58m.

The international highlight was world champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden handing Olympic champion Julien Alfred her first loss of the season to win the women's 100m, 10.78sec to 10.83.

title: Luxury cruise passengers left out of pocket after ship seized by receivers
text:
Customers who booked "once-in-a-lifetime" holidays to Western Australia's north have been left in limbo after a luxury cruise company went into administration.

Yet the high-end cruises to remote parts of the spectacular Kimberley coastline are still being advertised, and those with existing bookings say they have not been notified of the company's insolvency.

Receivers were appointed to Kimberley Pearl Tours (KPT) in January after sole director Daniel Brown, who took over the business in 2024, fell behind in repaying a loan he took out to help buy the business.

Bob Shawyer booked the "once-in-a-lifetime" trip with his wife. (Supplied: Bob Shawyer)

Bob Shawyer booked a KPT trip last year and is now $8,500 out of pocket.

"My wife and I didn't get a holiday we've been dreaming of," he said.

Mr Shawyer said he only discovered the trip was no longer going ahead by chance after an online search.

Cruises still advertised

Tours for the latter part of the year and for 2027 are still advertised on the KPT website and social media, including options to book the entire six-cabin vessel for $13,800 a night.

The website promises "one of the most memorable and incredible holidays of your life" and the cruises include chef-prepared meals and guided excursions with fishing equipment.

Ian Grant told the ABC he booked a private tour for a family trip and paid a "hefty" deposit.

Ian Grant booked a private boat tour for his family. (Supplied: Ian Grant)

The retired farmer said it was fortunate he discovered the company had gone into receivership before he received an invoice requesting $140,000 for the remainder of the booking.

"We could have paid that thinking it was hunky-dory," Mr Grant said.

Mr Shawyer said he also received an email requesting payment for the remainder of his booking after he discovered it was in receivership.

The invoices, seen by the ABC, were sent from the Kimberley Pearl email address about two to three months after receivers were appointed in January.

Private credit shortcomings

Mr Brown borrowed $395,000 from non-bank lender Blackbird Private Equity to help finalise his ownership of the company's sole charter vessel, the Kimberley Pearl, in 2024.

Blackbird is now under investigation by class action firm Adero Law over allegations of unfair lending practices to multiple customers.

Daniel Brown took over as Kimberley Pearl director in 2024. (Supplied: Daniel Brown)

Within 19 months, Mr Brown's loan debt was more than $1 million.

The matter is now before the Federal Court, where Mr Brown claims he was drawn into a predatory arrangement involving brokers, lenders and insolvency practitioners.

He said receivers had threatened to sell the Kimberley Pearl for less than market value after seizing the vessel in February.

Federal Court Justice Michael Feutrill last month imposed an order banning receivers from selling the company's assets, including the boat, pending further mediation of the matter by the parties.

He found there were questions over Blackbird's lending terms and the motivations behind its receivership appointments, although he made no definitive findings on these matters.

Hall Chadwick managing partner Richard Albarran is regularly appointed by Blackbird as a receiver.

Without deciding the issue, Justice Feutrill found it "reasonably arguable" on available affidavit evidence that the insolvency practitioner was appointed to KPT property in bad faith and not for a proper purpose.

Mr Brown alleged Mr Albarran was a "shadow director" of Blackbird, giving him motive to place "undue pressure" on KPT to refinance the loan.

The judge said evidence for that was "quite thin", but a family trust link between Mr Albarran and Blackbird might infer he had indirect interest in the lender's financial success.

Mr Albarran denied he was a shadow director of Blackbird in a statement to the ABC and said any suggestion he had used his position to gain advantage was "completely false".

The parties will next meet for mediation on August 31.

Deposits in limbo

Customers who paid deposits say they are no closer to getting their money back.

Justice Feutrill imposed an indefinite injunction banning Blackbird and receivers from selling KPT assets, including the boat. (Supplied: Daniel Brown)

Noel Blackmur said he was registered as an unsecured creditor but was not confident his deposit would be returned.

The Queensland holiday-maker said he was concerned by the lack of customer notification by receivers and administrators.

University of Sydney corporate law professor Jason Harris said the alleged silence was "very unusual".

"When I'm training newbie insolvency practitioners, that's a day one thing," he said.

Professor Harris said greater transparency in the private credit sector was needed.

"Regardless of the outcome, it [the case] will shine a light on the murky world of private credit," he said.

Jason Harris says the case could help to expose the "murky world" of private credit. (ABC News: Laurence Curson)

Hall Chadwick partner Brent Kijurina, who was also appointed to the property of KPT as a receiver, said customer notification was delayed because Mr Brown withheld the company's books and records.

"[This] required us to seek intervention from ASIC to obtain them," he said in a statement.

Mr Kijurina said receivers had not been provided with login information to update the KPT website or social media, and invoices for outstanding payments were sent by Mr Brown, not Hall Chadwick.

"This was done entirely without the knowledge, approval, or authorisation of the receivers," Mr Kijurina said.

He said customers who made payments after the receivers' appointment had been refunded, but some funds were withheld due to an "active court injunction".

Blackbird managing director Stewart Wilkinson said the company had not acted in bad faith.

He said Mr Brown had failed to make loan repayments for over 12 months and was "relying on future cruise deposits to pay creditors for cruises it had not undertaken".

Mr Wilkinson said Blackbird had also offered to settle Mr Brown's loan for less than the amount he borrowed.

Director defends allegations

Mr Brown denied sending invoices after the receivers' appointment, or withholding the company's books and records.

He said he had lived and operated the business aboard the Kimberley Pearl, which was seized in January with his personal belongings and company assets.

"It was therefore the receivers' own refusal of access that placed the books and records beyond reach," Mr Brown said in a statement.

Daniel Brown says it is his "firm intention" to get the Kimberley Pearl back on the water. (Supplied: Daniel Brown)

Mr Brown said it was his "firm intention" to get the Kimberley Pearl back in the water and refund customers, and was "deeply sorry".

"You trusted us with your holiday of a lifetime … that trust was broken by people who were never entitled to your money," he said.

title: Secretive, century-old explosives facility approved for expansion
text:
A secretive facility more than a century old has been approved for expansion, to meet increased demand from Australia's mining industry.

The Bajool Explosives Reserve, one of four state government-owned reserves, has expanded by more than 600 hectares since 2022 and will soon begin increasing its output.

"It's quite an important reserve for not just Queensland, but for the rest of Australia as well," said Rob White, Resources Safety and Health Queensland (RSHQ) explosives director.

"That's why we call it the 'Bajool in the Crown'.

"It's the gateway down to New South Wales and across to Western Australia as well."

The site, about 30 kilometres south of Rockhampton in Central Queensland, is used to store, manufacture and dispose of explosives mostly for the mining industry.

Rob White says the expansion is driven by increased demand. (Supplied)

Mr White confirmed among the materials stored at the high-security centre, were tonnes of ammonium nitrate, which can be made into ammonium nitrate emulsion, to be sent to mines around the country.

The exact amount of explosives and the security measures around them could not be confirmed, due to commercial in confidence and security concerns.

The facility also provides space for items including seized illegal fireworks, out-of-date ammunition and flares, to be safely destroyed inside large incinerators.

"It's about safe and secure explosives [that are] heavily regulated and secure to the community," Mr White said.

With its proximity to the Rockhampton Port, also known as Port Alma, the country's highest-volume licensed explosives port, precise operations inside the Bajool reserve have long been shrouded in secrecy.

Horses transporting wagons with explosives to the Bajool Explosives Reserve in 1956. (Supplied)

History and expansion plans

In addition to the Bajool site, the government has explosives reserves at White Rock near Cairns, Helidon near Brisbane and Brookhill near Townsville.

Bajool was originally gazetted for explosives purposes in the late 1800s and the site's first magazine, a structure designed to safely store or detonate explosives, was built in 1913.

In its infancy it was primarily used for the gold mine in Mount Morgan, about 60km away, and coal mine Blair Athol, more than 400km from the facility.

"Bajool has played an important part moving forward in history for the mining industry," Mr White said.

Explosives being transported between Bajool and Port Alma in the 1980s. (Supplied)

In 2022 the high-security site grew from 300 hectares to more than 900, using land to the north of the site to build more infrastructure.

As well as growing its physical size, in recent months it also received state government approval to increase operations.

It is the first major expansion of the reserve since it was established.

Mr White said the need for expansion was driven by increasing demand from the mining industry.

"We realised a number of years ago that we were running at capacity," he said.

"We can now bring industry in very shortly to then [see] at least a prospective site for manufacture and storage of ammonia nitrate."

An example of an explosives magazine in 1974 at Bajool. (Supplied)

CQ University resources engineering lecturer Xiaohan Yang agreed demand for more mining explosives was increasing.

"The upgrade [seems to be] not just for immediate demand, for also for future planning," Dr Yang said.

"Because of the need for the critical minerals and also the strategy for critical minerals from the Queensland government," he said.

Initial work at the expanded section will start early next year and it is expected to be fully operational by 2030.

With roughly 120 employees on site usually, the reserve's upgrade was expected to create an extra 50 to 70 direct jobs once operational, Mr White said.

"Then it could be anything up to 120 or more indirect jobs within the logistics chain itself, [such as] truck drivers," he said.

The facility has also previously been touted by a group of Central Queensland councils as one of the reasons the region was suitable for increased Australian Defence Force (ADF) infrastructure.

Mr White said though the reserve had stored for the ADF during past exercises, its focus remained on the mining industry.

title: Audiences flock to DIY shows as traditional live music venues struggle
text:
Craig Pieterson has been welcoming nearly 70 musicians a week into his Marrickville venue Lazybones Lounge for more than 13 years.

But with dwindling alcohol sales and rising costs, the model his cosy music bar is built on is not working like it used to.

"Everyone's doing it tough. I make more money on the door occasionally than I do over the bar and we've never seen that," Mr Pieterson said.

He said while audiences were still engaging with music, without bar spend to offset costs, the numbers did not add up.

"It's the bills that kills it," he said.

Alcohol sales are down at Craig Pieterson's Lazy Bones Lounge. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

Mr Pieterson is one of 33 recipients of a third round of New South Wales government grants aimed at propping up struggling venues following a spate of recent closures, including the nearby Moshpit Bar, Lazy Thinking and Mary's Underground.

"We're investing in the core music venues, venues that are playing five or six nights a week," Music and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham said.

"They're the ones employing musicians."

The venues, located across the state, will receive a share of $3.8 million for upgrades like soundproofing, new equipment, lighting and LED screens.

Focusing on screen and lighting, the government said, would help venues provide "compelling audiovisual experiences" to counter the competition from streaming, social media and other new media.

"For me to be better at providing a product that is of high-end world class, that's the only way I'd be able to achieve it," Mr Pieterson said.

Lazy Bones in Marrickvile is among 33 venues across NSW getting a cash injection. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

Growth of 'DIY' shows

But while traditional venues have been fighting to keep the lights on, bands performing in skate parks, backyards, warehouses and boxing gyms have been attracting enviable crowds.

The so-called "DIY" shows require a space and audience, and everything else is left up to the creativity of organisers.

They may or may not be ticketed, are often advertised through word of mouth or social media, and usually do not serve alcohol.

Warehouses are among the venues hosting DIY music events. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

At a DIY event in Marrickville, musicians performed in a boxing ring, and at another in Sydenham, the audience sat on the edges of a skate park while bands played inside the bowl.

At one event over the weekend, people danced around a giant egg in an Eveleigh warehouse.

One of the organisers, artist EJ Son, said the idea was born out of a chance meeting with fellow organiser and musician Grace Barr at an Ashfield sauna.

The pair spent two weeks recruiting other artists and musicians to help, borrowing sound equipment from friends, designing a line-up and installing two key artworks in the room.

"When it's just DIY with artists, there's a bit of an understanding of the need to be spontaneous and it's really special," EJ Son said.

Bands have been performing in boxing rings. (Supplied: Felix El James)

They have access to the space through an artist residency that is coming to an end, and while they were not exactly advertising the gig to owners, the potential for something "cool" was too tempting.

"I've got nothing to lose and it just needs to happen," they said.

Barr, who is a banjo player and singer, said getting consistent gigs had been difficult in Sydney.

"I think it is getting harder to find regular shows with venues that are able to offer a fee," Barr said.

While DIY gigs generally do not pay musicians, Barr said it was a chance to play in a less structured way instead of regimented sets.

"Maybe I want to experiment with playing for 30 minutes and then having a pause, and then someone's going to do a tap dance or someone's going to do a tap dance," the musician said.

"Which I think curators are interested in, but you don't have to ask for permission with a DIY show."

DIY shows offer musicians a less structured way to play. (Supplied: Felix El James)

Changing needs of audiences

Joe Hardy has been paying close attention to the DIY scene as part of his work as the co-founder of popular gig-guide SydneyMusic.Net.

He attributes much of the success of DIY shows to their creativity and sense of community.

"I think DIY is a lot more open-ended, and probably a lot more open-hearted as well, and I think that's what people are responding to and why the audiences are building at such a rate," Mr Hardy said.

Special entertainment precincts expand Taran Howard opened up his small bar in Sydney's inner west last September. Since then, he has learnt how to mix drinks "on the fly".

He said amid prolonged challenging conditions for venue owners, many have failed to remain attentive to changing audience sentiment.

"People talk a lot about reduction in drinking, but I actually think it's more nuanced and complex than that.

"People have different ideas around what they want to feel in terms of belonging in a space."

That can boil down to simple decisions like where people will sit and stand, where performers are positioned in a room, what hospitality is offered to attendees and how long people are invited to stay after the music ends.

"The number of occasions where we see people really doing very heartfelt and very accommodating, and warm hosting of people in their spaces, and that really changes the dynamics."

title: Calls for release of government review into short-stays amid Airbnb crisis
text:
As Sydney grapples with rising homelessness and low vacancy, local councils hold little power to act against short-term accommodation operators some say are draining the city's long-term rental supply.

Homelessness NSW has called for a 7.5 per cent levy on providers who rent out their properties on platforms such as Airbnb and Stayz, arguing it could generate millions to fund housing support services and free up extra rental stock.

In Sydney, where the vacancy rate sits at 2.1 per cent, there were 10,531 active Airbnb listings in August, according to market analysis from AirRoi.

City of Sydney Deputy Lord Mayor Jess Miller has supported the push for a crackdown on Airbnbs, but said limited data available to councils made it difficult to identify which were homes being lived in or investment properties being used solely for short-term accommodation.

Jess Miller is concerned short-stay investors could buy up new residential apartment blocks without stronger regulation. (ABC News: Nandini Dhir)

Cr Miller said with thousands of new dwellings flagged under the housing delivery authority, nothing was preventing investors from exploiting new residential developments "to in effect rezone them to commercial, by solely using them as accommodation properties".

"The mythology of the solution to the problem is more supply is completely eroded when you look at what the supply that we have is actually being used for," she said.

In 2021, the state government introduced an 180-day cap on short-term rentals where hosts do not occupy the entire home, and required all properties in the sector to be registered to track compliance breaches.

There are more than 10,000 Airbnbs in Sydney, according to market analysis. (ABC News: Millie Roberts)

But Cr Miller said because information on the short-term rental accommodation (STRA) database was only accessible by the state government, local councils had limited enforcement capability.

"The government needs to be able to provide us a database that is completely transparent, that identifies properties, their ownership status, their use status, the nights that they are being rented out on and the revenue being generated," she said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure told the ABC that councils were responsible for enforcing planning laws relating to individual properties, including short-term accommodation rentals.

The spokesperson said the department provided quarterly data from the NSW STRA register to Airbnb at its request to understand how short-term rental activity was changing across council areas over time.

At this stage, no other booking platforms had made requests for this data, the spokesperson added.

Sydney is grappling with rising homelessness and low vacancy. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Council investigates ban

The City of Sydney is considering a ban on short-term rental accommodation in areas where concentration is high, or where vacancy rates fall below 3 per cent.

The Greens-led proposal estimated the move could return up to 5,000 properties to the long-term rental market.

Greens Councillor Sylvie Ellsmore said in Millers Point, where public housing was sold off by the former Coalition government, the situation was "particularly grotesque".

"Most of those homes used to be public housing, [they] used to be where low-income people could live," she said.

"Now they are Airbnbs … which represents a huge failure of government policy."

Sylvie Ellsmore reflected on the rise of short-stay rentals in Millers Point. (Supplied)

The Greens believe the proposal could return up to 5,000 properties to the long-term rental. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Cr Ellsmore said the impact of Airbnbs in the area had led to the closure of a historic childcare centre due to dwindling enrolments, and believed no fines had ever been issued for enforcement breaches.

"Councils want to do things that their community needs, but we're very restricted under the current laws unless the state government changes them," she said.

A spokesperson for Airbnb ANZ told the ABC the vast majority of its listed properties were primary residences and homes used periodically by their owners.

An Airbnb spokesperson says the majority of its listed properties are primary residences used periodically by owners. (Flickr)

The spokesperson said Airbnb remained committed to being a constructive partner to the City of Sydney during its proposal but added, "successful policy must target chronic undersupply, which is the primary driver of the housing crisis".

Stayz senior director of government and corporate affairs, Eacham Curry, said the company supported "fit-for-purpose regulation" of the STRA sector.

Mr Curry said any levy introduced should be of "a reasonable level" and "applied uniformly to all short-term accommodation providers".

Local councils hold limited enforcement capability to act against short-stay accommodation investors who break the rules. (ABC News: Miriah Davis)

Delays to short-term rental accommodation review

Both Cr Ellsmore and Cr Miller queried the release of the government's review into STRA, which they described as "massively overdue" and potentially "outdated".

Premier Chris Minns vowed to crack down on the issue amid the housing crisis, with a review into the STRA sector announced in 2024.

"We don't know if it's finished, we don't know when they're going to release it, we don't know what it's going to say," Cr Ellsmore said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was unable to confirm a release date, but said the government was in "the process of finalising" the review.

A review into the STRA sector was announced in 2024. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

A spokesperson for the NSW government said any changes to short-term accommodation would need to consider impacts on the tourism sector and housing affordability.

"The government is currently reviewing the operation of the short-term rental accommodation planning and regulatory framework and will make announcements in due course," they said.

Solutions to the problem 'complex'

Short Term Accommodation Association Australia (STAAA) executive director Keiran Craig-Jones said there was no evidence nightly caps worked and that prohibition would punish compliant operators.

He said the main issue was the rental arbitrage model, where a third party leases a home to sublet it for a significant profit, which was leading to genuine long-term rental housing being lost.

"Those operators are typically not local, have no vested interest in the local area and community and no relationship with the neighbours who deal with the consequences," he said.

The peak body, he said, therefore supported a ban on the practice with a focus on "enforcement, registration and data-sharing" instead.

Caitlin Buckle, a lecturer in City Planning at the University of New South Wales, said stricter regulations may not necessarily encourage property owners to move into the long-term market.

Caitlin Buckle says really strict regulations may deter people from offering their homes. (Supplied: Anna Kucera)

"Really strict regulations may actually just prevent people from offering their homes to anyone at all rather than them necessarily changing their minds and offering it onto the long-term market," Professor Buckle said.

To regulate the sector effectively, it was important to consider the local area, short-term rental habits, financial feasibility and the reasoning for letting out properties, she explained.

"I think one of the key challenges would be to getting really good data … that's a really important starting place from being able to actually anticipate what different regulations might look like and what the impact of those regulations might be, just because it can be very complex," she said.

A young local family paid $3.92 million for a charming clinker brick house in Kew at auction on Saturday, beating a buyer’s agent in what the selling agent called one of the first competitive auctions he had seen in months. The five-bedroom home at 22 Ridgeway Avenue dates to about 1935 and retains its heritage character but has been updated and converted from a duplex into a family home with a gourmet kitchen, outdoor entertaining area, large windows and a landscaped garden. The property was one of 570 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 58 per cent from 365 reported results throughout the week, while 67 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Two parties competed for the Kew home, which had been listed with a price guide of $3.5 million to $3.8 million.

Kay & Burton selling agent Scott Patterson said other potential buyers attended but did not get a chance to bid. Young families were the main demographic interested in the home, he said, noting it had several drawcards. “I think the charm and character of the 1930s era, big rooms and solid brick construction,” he said. “Five bedrooms, three bathrooms, so it was a little bit more accommodation than you would usually find.

The UK public are not clamouring for the couple’s return to the fold. Brits are, at best, divided by their return. As a British-born journalist who has written for the UK tabloid Harry sued – The Sun – and other Murdoch titles, I should be Harry’s bête noire. After a successful summer seafood pop-up at Stokehouse’s beachfront kiosk in St Kilda, and recent months cooking and eating her way around Morocco, Italy and the Netherlands, ex-Hope St Radio chef Ellie Bouhadana is launching her own restaurant. Dafina Seaside Grill will open in the storied Claypots site in St Kilda in early 2027, adding extra verve to an exciting time for the suburb, with Andrew McConnell’s Trader House taking over Stokehouse in spring and new developments happening on down-at-heel Fitzroy Street. Chef Ellie Bouhadana and husband Rapha Tamir will open Dafina Seaside Grill in the former Claypots site. Simon Schluter “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us,” says Bouhadana, who lives locally and is working alongside husband Rapha Tamir. “My parents brought me to Acland Street when I was a kid, for ice-cream, cakes and Luna Park. We came to Claypots, too. We couldn’t let it be gutted, maybe turned into a KFC.” Tamir’s grandparents came for regular Friday spaghetti marinara lunches and he remembers long meals under the courtyard’s bougainvillea. “It felt celebratory, with a casual, affordable approach to seafood,” he says.

1 / 3 The enormous octopus that once hung from Claypots’ ceiling. Erin Slattery 2 / 3 The bar of Claypots in January 2007, with seahorse door handles visible (right). Erin Slattery 3 / 3 Ellie Bouhadana and Rapha Tamir with the quirky Claypots doors. Simon Schluter Previous Slide Next Slide Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Renan Goksin opened Claypots in 1998, serving gumbos, chilli crab and simple grills. The atmosphere was bohemian, musical and charmingly chaotic. Neelam Sami took over in 2016 and Claypots remained a grungy slice of old-time St Kilda until it closed in February. Goksin has pointed out special features to the restaurant’s new custodians, who will retain some in their new fit-out. “He told me the bar is made from stolen pieces of the old St Kilda pier, so that’s non-negotiable,” says Tamir. Canvas sails are suspended from rope pulleys as de facto air-conditioning. Carved seahorses double as door handles. Walls are stuck with faux Sumerian tablets etched with cuneiform (the world’s oldest-known writing system), clustered around one that is apparently real. An enormous pressed tin octopus hangs from the ceiling – a head-scraping hazard, but also an icon. “We like the quirks and the energy but we’ll do our own thing,” says Tamir. “It’s going to be Ellie’s food, but we do feel attracted to St Kilda institutions and the Jewish immigrant story here.”

Advertisement

It will be the debut restaurant of chef Ellie Bouhadana (right), in partnership with Rapha Tamir. Simon Schluter Dafina is named for a Sephardi Jewish slow-cooked meat-and-grain dish that speaks to Bouhadana’s Jewish Moroccan heritage. “It’s a claypot cooked overnight in the communal fire, in the embers of the dying coals,” she says. In Jewish culture, foods are often slowly cooked on Friday night’s cooling fire, ready for the Sabbath when cooking is not allowed. “We’ll also do Moroccan-style brochette [kebabs], whole fish with cumin and garlic, lamb chops, dips and salad, lots of oil and vinegar, food for swiping with fresh-baked flatbreads.” Related Article How to make one of Melbourne’s favourite focaccias at home Bouhadana first came to attention for her lockdown pop-ups, including pasta parties and sandwiches sold from her driveway. She was the first chef at Collingwood wine-slash-listening bar Hope St Radio in 2021, and took the restaurant to a hat in the 2023 Age Good Food Guide. “I’ve been nervous to commit to a site,” she says. “But what I love about pop-ups is working with interesting people who become friends as we explore each other’s food and hosting style. It’s exciting to think about sharing my own hospitality. There’s a renewal in St Kilda, and we’re excited to put down roots and be part of that.” Dafina Seaside Grill opens early 2027 at 213 Barkly Street, St Kilda.

A century-old house with shagpile carpet and mustard-coloured lino that has never changed hands has now sold for a reserve-smashing $3.225 million. Perched on an 899-square-metre parcel with city views, the unrenovated three-bedroom house at 74 Agnes Street in Auchenflower was described as one of the last of its kind. Beneath its peeling mid-century wallpaper, it offered a prime piece of land with three-street frontage and a subdivision opportunity that could see it split into two corner lots in what is now Brisbane’s third-most expensive suburb. Seven buyers – representing a mix of developers and owner-occupiers – registered for the Saturday auction and six bid. A Redcliffe family kicked off bidding at $2.1 million, sparking a developer to quickly counter with $2.52 million.

Advertisement

“We had a few buyers hesitating after that,” said selling agent Josh Brown, of Ray White Collective. “That brought the price pretty close to the reserve, so we paused and then called it on the market.” The three-bedroom house at 74 Agnes Street is perched on an 899-square-metre parcel with city views. Ray White It sparked a flurry of more than 100 rises ranging between $500 and $25,000, including one eyebrow-raising bid of $2,842,368.74. Yet even that precise rise didn’t slow momentum. At $3.225 million the hammer dropped and a local family claimed the keys.

“They were so happy,” Brown said. “It’s a pretty unique house with a northern aspect on a big allotment surrounded by beautiful homes. The carpet and wallpaper could do with an update but didn’t stymie interest in the house. Ray White “And it’s untouched … it was owned by the same family for 100 years. There are not many homes like this left here.” The auction came weeks after Auchenflower muscled its way into Brisbane’s top-three priciest suburbs. Domain’s June House Price Report showed house medians skyrocketed 26.1 per cent in 12 months to $2.175 million.

While the pocket’s pulling power underpinned the result, Brown said buyer confidence had also crept back. The home was one of 153 scheduled auctions across south-east Queensland. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 20 per cent from 94 reported results, with 16 homes withdrawn. In Hawthorne, a two-bedroom, one-bathroom townhouse sold for $1.02 million after three active bidders battled for the keys. A woman who had sold her place in Newstead six months earlier, and was living with a friend, claimed the prize. Perched on a 169-square-metre lot in a complex of six, the townhouse at 2/71 Miles Street features a balcony, yard and a recently upgraded bathroom. It last sold two years ago for $826,000.

Seven bidders registered and three competed after the auction opened at $900,000. After an early pause, a vendor bid of $1 million sparked a few more rises until it sold. Selling agent Eliza Schultz, of Place Bulimba, said the price was a record for the complex and highlighted the strong buyer competition at that price point. “This was one of the strongest auctions we’ve had in a while … we had really good engagement from day one,” she said. “Townhouses are performing very well at the moment, especially in blue chip areas like Hawthorne.”

Schultz said the home attracted single couples, first-home buyers, upsizers and a few investors, adding that the owner’s pre-auction prep added to the strong interest. “He did everything we recommended … including a fresh lick of paint, updating the carpet and a basic bathroom renovation,” she said. “It looked flawless. It cost him probably $25,000 to $30,000 but it meant any buyers coming through knew there was nothing to do.” In Ascot, an iconic family estate built in the ’90s sold under the hammer for $5.25 million to a local buyer who only set foot in the home just 24 hours beforehand. Sydney Swans’ assistant Mark McVeigh will present to the Essendon board on Monday ahead of his expected endorsement as senior coach, as club great James Hird expressed his disappointment at missing out on the job. The 45-year-old McVeigh was in the coaches’ box as the Swans defeated North Melbourne in an emotional encounter at the SCG but will be in Melbourne to make a final presentation to the board before his appointment is confirmed, according to two industry sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity. After retiring in 2012 he moved back to NSW where he became an assistant coach at the Giants, and served as the club’s interim coach after Leon Cameron stood down in 2022. The service will continue on SBS On Demand with additional bulletins.

SBS WorldWatch will soon become a digital-only service, ending its run as a broadcast television channel.

The multilingual news service, which provides news bulletins from international broadcasters, will move entirely to SBS On Demand.

SBS says the shift will allow it to increase the number of bulletins available in most languages.

SBS WorldWatch to move online only
