title: The hidden underbelly of Australia's weight-loss drug boom
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

This article contains references to eating disorders.

For Kansasin Darwan, living in Bajool in central Queensland, the weight-loss injection was supposed to be a solution. Instead, she says, it left her barely able to function.

I was dizzy, nauseous, and I lost my appetite. To put it simply, I could barely live.

The 48-year-old says she had gained weight during perimenopause and believed her Australian GP was unlikely to prescribe a weight-management medicine because she did not meet the relevant clinical criteria.

In Australia, GLP-1 weight loss drugs are generally prescribed for chronic weight management in adults with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, or a BMI of 27 to under 30 with at least one weight-related health condition.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

So, while on holiday in her home country of Thailand, Darwan went to a beauty clinic in outer Bangkok and bought an injectable medicine branded as Mounjaro.

Beauty clinics in Thailand are generally supervised by doctors. However, the screening process for GLP-1 use can be less extensive than the assessment typically conducted by GPs in Australia. For example, some customers at beauty clinics may be prescribed GLP-1 drugs even if they do not have diabetes or are within a healthy weight range.

Darwan brought the drugs back to Australia and began using them to lose weight.

"I couldn't concentrate while driving. I wasn't feeling like myself. I couldn't sleep. Even my children noticed that I was different," she tells SBS Thai.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration has issued multiple safety advisories regarding the importation of unregistered GLP-1 products promoted online for weight loss. Source: PA / Niall Carson

Eighteen out of every 1,000 Australians, or almost 2 per cent of the population, are now taking GLP-1s regularly, according to a study by scientists at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) published in November 2025.

Darwan's experience offers a glimpse into a fast-growing market for weight-loss injections, where some Australians are seeking access overseas, while others are obtaining medicines through social-media sellers and informal supply channels.

An investigation by SBS Thai found weight-loss medicines being offered without a doctor's prescription in Australian community groups, reports of products entering the country through informal channels, and unapproved peptides being marketed as weight-loss products.

But access to these medicines is not uniformly occurring outside the established medical system. Many Australians obtain weight-loss drugs through registered health professionals and pharmacies.

For consumers navigating this market, the distinction between an approved prescription medicine, an experimental drug and an unapproved product can be difficult to see — with experts and authorities warning that using medicines outside approved pathways can carry serious risks.

The unregulated supply chain

For some consumers, access does not require a trip overseas.

SBS Thai found GLP-1 injectable medicines openly advertised in Australian Thai community Facebook groups, with some sellers offering the products without requiring a prescription.

We contacted one Melbourne-based seller, posing as a potential customer interested in buying "Mounjaro". The seller offered a 5mg vial for $750, saying it had been sourced from a beauty clinic in Udon Thani, a provincial city in north-east Thailand.

We contacted the clinic identified by the seller, which confirmed that it supplied products to the Melbourne-based seller.

SBS Thai has not independently established the circumstances of every shipment or whether every product sold through the channel was imported in accordance with Australian requirements.

The price for the 5mg multi-dose pre-filled injection pen also appeared significantly higher than the price we found for the same branded medicine at Australian pharmacies, where it was listed between $375 and $415 depending on the pharmacy and required a prescription.

The seller's claim of easy access raises significant regulatory and health concerns.

In response to an SBS Thai query, a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) spokesperson said: "It is not legal to import GLP-1 medicines or peptide products into Australia for commercial purposes without appropriate authorisation and declaration."

The spokesperson said GLP-1 receptor agonists, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are prescription-only medicines in Australia and should be used under the supervision of a qualified health professional.

The regulator has also warned about unregistered products being sold as GLP-1 medicines, particularly those obtained online or from overseas.

In March, TGA testing found several imported products labelled as containing GLP-1 or GLP-1 analogues contained none of those ingredients. The regulator advised consumers to obtain prescription medicines from registered Australian pharmacies rather than social media or other digital platforms.

The regulator has also increased its focus on unapproved peptide products.

Earlier this month, with assistance from NSW Police, the TGA seized more than $120,000 worth of unapproved peptide and anabolic steroid products from two NSW properties. The TGA said the products had allegedly been imported, relabelled and promoted for sale through social media and a website.

One of the products seized was labelled "retatrutide" — a name that also appeared in SBS Thai's investigation.

We found retatrutide offered at $300 for a 10mg vial at a Thai grocery store in Geelong, Victoria. The seller claimed the injectable product could help with weight loss and work similarly to other GLP-1 medicines.

A poster at a Thai grocery store in Victoria reads: "Weight loss injections and citizenship mock tests available here." Source: SBS News / Atitaya Teepawat

Retatrutide is different from approved GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy. While those medicines contain semaglutide, retatrutide is an experimental drug that acts on three hormone pathways involved in appetite and metabolism. It is not approved for sale as a medicine in Australia.

SBS Thai did not independently test the product or establish what was inside the vial. The TGA says unapproved peptide products have not been evaluated for safety, quality or effectiveness.

There is also a separate health warning involving products labelled retatrutide.

In June, Victoria's Department of Health said it had been notified of six cases of acute liver injury since January among people who had used products labelled as retatrutide. The department said investigations were continuing.

Demand is surging

The informal market is emerging alongside a rapid increase in legitimate use of GLP-1 medicines.

Researchers at UNSW found that total sales of GLP-1 medicines rose from about 58,000 in May 2020 to 500,000 in April 2025. They also noted a significant disruption in sales from late 2022 to early 2024, when a drug shortage caused sales to drop by almost 80 per cent.

The researchers found that private, non-subsidised access had grown sharply, accounting for 43.8 per cent of estimated use by April 2025, with prices up to $600 per month.

The study did not include Wegovy and Saxenda, which are marketed specifically for weight loss. The researchers said their figures should therefore be regarded as a minimum estimate of overall GLP-1 use.

Source: SBS News

That expanding market is also being discussed heavily on social media.

Like Darwan, Ople Petchdee, who lives in Croydon South in Melbourne's east, also bought a GLP-1 injectable from a beauty clinic just outside the Thai capital, Bangkok.

Petchdee, who has called Australia home for the past 15 years, says she became interested in the medicines after seeing friends post about their experiences.

"Everyone posted on their Facebook, on their social media, that these medications helped them lose weight. So, my friends suggested I use them, too," she tells SBS Thai.

Beyond the weight-loss promise

For Trevor Steward, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Melbourne, the concern is not only how people obtain GLP-1 medicines but also how the drugs are presented and understood online.

Associate professor Trevor Steward is running a clinical trial examining how GLP-1 drugs affect the neurobiological function of people with eating disorders. Source: Supplied / Trevor Steward

Steward is currently running a clinical trial examining how GLP-1 drugs affect the neurobiological function of people with binge eating disorder.

It's not about aesthetics. It's not about achieving a certain number on a scale.

"It's about someone's mental and physical wellbeing. And that's something that needs to be considered holistically with a doctor involved," Steward tells SBS Thai.

He says there are also unanswered questions about what happens when treatment stops for people with eating disorders.

"If the weight comes back, we can maybe stipulate that the food noise will come back. And how will that person cope with that, thinking that they have achieved a certain sense of recovery and then falling back into that old pattern of behaviour before."

Steward says social media often strips away that nuance, framing GLP-1 medicines as a shortcut to achieving a particular body shape or weight, rather than treating them as serious medications to be considered in the context of a person's overall mental and physical health.

For Darwan, who had gone looking for a way to lose weight, reality was harder.

"My mood was depressing. I suffered from energy loss."

I will not use [GLP-1 drugs] again.

title: One Nation MP admits the party's true migration target 'isn't too different' from Labor's
text:
in brief Pauline Hanson has rejected claims on immigration made by her own MP.

David Farley conceded the party's overall intake numbers are not too different from Labor's forecasts.

One Nation's immigration stance is under question after an MP said the party would include an extra 100,000 people annually in its policy — bringing its target total higher than present forecasts under Labor.

Farrer MP David Farley, who clinched Sussan Ley's old seat from the coalition at a by-election, told the ABC Insiders program on Sunday morning that his party had decided to separate a "true NOM", or net overseas migration figure, from certain other categories of migrants.

However, party leader Pauline Hanson was forced to quickly intervene, refuting the claims just hours later on social media. Party policy is to "cut net overseas migration to 130,000".

"One Nation's target is less than half of Labor's current level," she wrote.

This contradicts messaging from Farley, who said One Nation's stated policy of getting net overseas migration down to 130,000 excluded people brought in under a Pacific scheme, aged-care nurses and other in-demand skilled workers.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Adding those groups would amount to an additional 100,000 arrivals, bringing the total to 230,000 — 5,000 more than the budget forecast of 225,000 in the coming four years.

"What we're doing is we're focusing on the NOM in its true form, and then we've got these programs that have been available now for over a decade that drive our economy," Farley told Insiders.

"The raw number is not too different, but the reality is, where do we need them?

"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."

One Nation 'effectively backing' Labor's plan

The comments come as public debate continues around the optimum level of migration to Australia.

Net overseas migration dropped to 306,000 in 2024-25, brought down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000 under Liberal-National government policy.

Cabinet minister Chris Bowen said net overseas migration could not just be redefined.

"My overwhelming conclusion was he's pretty comfortable with what the government's doing," Bowen told reporters.

"I'm not sure what campaign One Nation's going to run on migration if they're effectively backing in what the Albanese government is doing."

Opposition immigration spokesman Jonno Duniam said voters were owed a clear explanation of what the party's immigration policy actually is.

"These are not semantic distinctions. They have real consequences for housing, infrastructure, essential services, wages, jobs and the economy," he said.

"For a party that has spent years telling Australians it has all the answers on immigration, One Nation is having extraordinary difficulty answering the most basic question of all: how many migrants would actually come to Australia under its policy."

Opinion polls have shown that voters trust One Nation to manage migration better than the two major parties.

Hanson says One Nation's cuts will come from "fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs".

David Farley won One Nation's first lower house seat in the Farrer by-election in May, securing an unprecedented 32.9 percent swing. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

"Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration," she wrote.

Individuals must stay in Australia for 12 months in a 16-month period to be included in NOM figures, meaning short-term seasonal workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme are typically not counted.

Long-term workers on the same scheme are counted, as are backpakers and working holiday makers who typically stay in the country for more than a year.

Hanson will test racial discrimination laws in the High Court.

The confusion comes as Hanson declared she would take her racial discrimination challenge with Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to the High Court.

The senator lost a Federal Court appeal last month against a ruling which found her in breach of racial vilification laws after she told the Greens senator to "piss off back to Pakistan".

Asked if racial discrimination laws should be changed, Farley said he wasn't convinced they should be.

He said his leader's comments "can be taken as an insult" but weren't inciting racial discrimination.

"Hanson's got every right to challenge it," Farley said.

"I think if we went through the pub test, I know which way it would go. It'd go in Pauline's favour."

This is the second time Hanson has had to correct comments made by Farley after he said he would display both the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags alongside the Australian flag at his electorate office.

One Nation's policy is to only fly the Australian flag on public buildings. Hanson has described having multiple official flags as "extremely divisive".

title: 'We support the club': Sydney Swans' fans stay loyal amid scandal engulfing men’s side
text:
In brief The Sydney Swans have played their first game since being rocked by a sexual assault scandal.

A planned walk out of the men's game proved more of a trickle than a mass exodus.

The Sydney Swans AFLW team has set a new attendance record, with fans warmly welcoming them to the field despite a major sexual assault scandal engulfing the men's side.

Attendance reached 16,672 spectators on Sunday afternoon, a new record for the women's club which more than doubles the previous record of 8,264.

The Swans AFLW team played their second-ever game at the Sydney Cricket Ground (SCG) on Sunday in a history double-header before the men took to the field.

A planned mass walk-out of fans ahead of the men's match failed to materialise as large crowds remained for both games. A small stream of supporters, some waving placards, did exit the SCG prior to the men's game, various media reported.

Five Swans players, including elite players Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner, have been suspended for the remainder of the AFL season for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late.

Several fans told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency that they still supported the club despite feeling disappointed in players involved in the scandal.

"We support the club wholeheartedly," Swans supporter Russell Le-Guier said.

"The club itself is what this is about, not the individual players, they'll come and go over the years, but it's the club itself that we support."

The Swans AFLW team doubled their crowd attendance record during only their second time playing at the SCG. Source: Getty / Cameron Spencer

Sydney Swans Chairman Andrew Pridham said: "The five players made a terrible mistake."

"However, they are part of our club, and as such we will do everything in our power to care for them," he said during a pre-game event.

"We do not excuse their behaviour. We do not ignore the impact it has had on so many people — and in particular women."

Don't punish the other players, fans say

Speaking with AAP, several fans said they were supportive of the men on the field.

Rosalie Le-Guier said she'd be cheering just as loud, if not louder than usual, when the men took the field.

"You don't punish the boys in the rest of the team," she said.

"We're here to support the club. We're here to support the rest of the players."

Another Swans fan, Kate Hipsley said she wouldn't be walking out of the stadium.

"As far as we know, the men playing in the men's game have not done anything wrong and they will be hurting as well," she said.

"I don't care about the premiership — it's more important than premierships — you care for the culture of the team, which has taken a huge hit."

Supporter David McGilchrist said he was generally happy with how the club had dealt with the scandal, despite being disappointed.

"I'm disappointed, and I've got a bit of anger now as well of what's happened, but a lot of disappointment and massive shock," he said.

"But I'm here to support the girls, the men, the club."

'Healing and moving forward'

Pridham said the club intends to rebuild trust in the community.

"While we are deeply shocked and disappointed with what transpired, we believe that since it occurred, we have acted with honesty, dignity and urgency," he said.

"Now we begin the process of healing and moving forward."

That will involve a better understanding of "how our cultural pillars failed to prevent such a thing from happening", he elaborated.

Investigation continues

Three women at the centre of the alleged sexual assault scandal have not spoken publicly as they consider potential civil claims.

It's understood the women joined players at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after the Swans' win over Essendon last Sunday night.

One of the trio, who has engaged personal injury specialists Slater and Gordon, was navigating an "incredibly traumatic experience", according to senior attorney Jackson Pannam.

He says the firm has been asked to determine whether the woman, who has put multiple sexual assault allegations to police, has grounds to file a civil claim.

Pannam said the woman contacted police immediately after the alleged assaults and that her world had been turned upside down.

Another law firm is also reportedly helping two of the women prepare to launch action in the Victorian Supreme Court.

''We are currently investigating the circumstances and preparing to commence legal proceedings against the club and potentially the individuals involved,'' Carbone Lawyers partner Manny Carbone told The Age on Friday.

Fellow lawyer John Karantzis said the two women he represented were suffering severe stress and anxiety and feared for their lives after being subjected to "abhorrent actions".

"There's a lot of interest in this case and they are literally in hiding and they are suffering," he told Melbourne radio station 3AW.

Karantzi claimed more than five men were in the room at the Pullman but refused to comment when asked if coaches were present.

The Swans have "categorically" denied any of their staff were in the hotel room and said none are involved in the investigation.

The AFL's integrity unit is also investigating.

title: From Adelaide to Hull, the Socceroos star who could be football’s next big thing
text:
in brief The Queenslander was thrown into the action with Hull leading 2-0.

Hull's victory was their first league triumph over United since 1974.

Australian teenager Lucas Herrington has made a stunning arrival in the Premier League, coming off the bench to help Hull City pull off a famous 2-0 boilover against Manchester United.

The 18-year-old Socceroo, the only Australian currently playing in England's top flight, was thrown into the deep end when starting defender Nobel Mendy went off injured in the 64th minute.

The record $33 million Australian signing barely put a foot wrong as Hull held firm to claim their first league win over United in 52 years.

Written off as overwhelming relegation favourites, with former England Joe Cole irritating their fans with his suggestion that "Hull are gone, man", the Yorkshire side were well worth their win over a lumbering United whose build-up play was too pedestrian and attacking execution too shoddy.

In the 38th minute the Tigers' central defender Nobel Mendy, signed on the same day as Herrington earlier in the month but who got the nod to start ahead of the young Aussie, scored their second goal.

By that time, Michael Carrick's United were already struggling to get to grips with a side that deservedly led through a couple of first-half set-pieces.

Centre-back Semi Ajayi opened the scoring in the 17th minute when United failed to deal with a corner, and then Regan Slater whipped in a 38th-minute free-kick that another central defender, Mendy, latched onto, nodding home expertly.

With Hull's Bosnian boss Sergej Jakirovic revealing that Ajayi, Mendy and captain Lewis Coyle will all have to be assessed for their injuries over the next 24 hours, Herrington will next be in line to feature in Wednesday AEST's League Cup tie at Championship side Stoke.

title: They rejected the Aussie dream. What they bought instead cost $130,000
text:
A sprawling property with a white picket fence was once a symbol of success, but for Lizzie Villestas this version of home ownership is a trap, not a triumph.

"For many, success is measured by the square footage of your property and for us, we began to see large homes as a different kind of trap; one that comes with massive debt and endless maintenance," Villestas told SBS Chinese.

For more than three years, she has lived in a tiny house measuring just eight metres long and 2.5 metres wide, or 20 square metres. The average floor area of a new house in Australia was 232.3 square metres in 2021/22, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Villestas' space may be small, but it's been thoughtfully designed, featuring a deep green and timber colour palette, akin to the surrounding bushland. It's even fitted with a study loft, bathtub and an indoor fireplace.

A labour of love, the property was constructed by Villestas and David Menhennett over 18 months and cost about $130,000. The couple now live in north-east Victoria and can relocate their tiny house on wheels across Australia, as desired.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It was a virtual no-brainer ... most Australians are looking down the barrel of now ... a 30-year mortgage of up to a million dollars to own an average home," said Menhennett, who previously lived in Hong Kong for around 20 years.

Compounded by Australia's housing crisis, experts believe demand for tiny houses is surging. But while these properties promise big savings, they're often associated with regulatory red tape and financing complexities.

A dwelling, a vehicle or both?

Driven by a desire to achieve financial freedom, Danielle Lester decided to adopt tiny house living two years ago.

She now serves as president of the volunteer-run Australian Tiny Homes Association (ATHA) but admits it's difficult to gather robust data about the number of tiny homes in Australia.

"Our membership base doesn't fully represent the amount of people who are living in tiny homes around Australia, and we find because of the regulatory complexity, a lot of people are choosing to do it under the radar, at their own risk," Lester told SBS News.

"Obviously, people have got no other option at the moment but to find a roof to put over their heads."

In part, that's because there's no official national definition for what constitutes a tiny house in Australia. Instead, they are regulated by federal, state and local government authorities — whose planning policies can often overlap and contradict each other.

Griffith University emeritus professor Paul Burton said tiny homes are also classified differently depending on their design.

That includes tiny houses fixed to the ground, which is "like a conventional house only smaller".

Burton told SBS News the image that usually comes to mind when people think of these properties is a tiny house on wheels:

"So, that's something that can be hitched to a truck or car and moved a bit like a caravan. They are treated under a lot of legislation or local laws passed by councils ... like a caravan, even though they're not really the same."

The tiny houses market in Australia has evolved to offer affordable, mid-tier and high end designs to cater to the growing clientele. Credit: Lizzie Villestas and David Menhennett

In NSW, one caravan can legally be installed on a property without council approval if it is connected with and occupied by members of the owner's household.

If a person is staying longer-term on land they do not own, they typically need council approval. In NSW, this usually involves submitting a development application and, in some cases, engineering certificates about the structural safety of a tiny home on wheels.

In June, Shellharbour City Council on the south coast of NSW announced it would take a different approach. It has adopted a two-year trial program which removes the need for a development application for tiny houses used as rental accommodation.

In 2025, Bega Valley Shire Council — also in NSW — issued a compliance order asking that a tiny house on wheels it deemed unauthorised be demolished. Owners of the tiny house have since lodged an appeal through the NSW Land and Environment Court.

Burton believes local council approaches are "inconsistent" and said ATHA is working on a national advocacy strategy to "help unpack the complexity of the tiny house world".

Financing for tiny houses

Jamie Mitchell is a senior broker at Great Escape Finance and told SBS News that because tiny houses on wheels are not classified as dwellings, they are not eligible for home loans.

He said another "hurdle" is that not all tiny houses follow the same construction codes, so for a long time lenders wouldn't take security over the property.

"There's no guarantee that the person who built the tiny home has done a good job. So, there are definitely builders that have been around and now have a good reputation. But from a lender's point of view, they're still quite risk-averse."

Mitchell said his company now works with several personal and commercial loan lenders to enable financing for tiny houses. Generally, the maximum loan term for a personal loan is up to seven years.

Last year, Commonwealth Bank also announced it would become the first major bank to offer a construction loan for prefabricated houses.

When asked whether demand for tiny house financing has grown in recent years, Mitchell laughed and admitted, "I'm just so swamped at the moment, it's just ridiculous."

"To give you an idea, our record for the amount of turnover that we did in a month historically, in March this year we more than doubled that ... and every month since has been pretty close to what that original record was."

Mitchell's clients were typically single women "that might have been divorced and were heading towards retirement". Now, the demographic has shifted to include more young families and single professionals planning to live permanently in tiny houses.

A risky investment?

According to the ATHA, a professionally built tiny house on wheels can cost between $80,000 and more than $170,000 depending on the size, design and customisation of the property.

But unlike traditional houses, which tend to increase in value after purchase, Burton cautioned that tiny houses on wheels can depreciate over time.

"When we talk about increasing house prices, what's typically increasing is the land value, not the structure itself ... so, a tiny house on wheels unless it's very special ... it's probably going to diminish or at best hold its value."

Lester believes the amount she is paying to rent land for her tiny house is significantly cheaper than rental accommodation she has experienced in the past.

"Not only that, I've got full control over my environment, my living situations, my surroundings," she said.

Like a caravan, a tiny house on wheels can be relocated as required. Credit: Lizzie Villestas and David Menhennett

"This cost of living crisis affects everybody, landlords included, which can have knock-on effects on their ability to maintain your property in an adequate way. So, I think savings to be had from living in a tiny house and renting land are significant."

For Villestas, who previously lived in Hong Kong in a small apartment, tiny living is not just a cost-saving measure, but a lifestyle choice.

"There is a growing community that is going towards this alternative living because of the pressures that the housing crisis is causing at the moment. It just gives the future generations a little bit of hope, to be able to own ... buy and own a property.

"You've just got to have an open mind if you want to live the way that we live, but it is certainly possible."

title: 'Obesity paradox': Study finds common health metric could be misleading for older people
text:
Key Points A "normal" BMI does not necessarily indicate low health risk, particularly when accompanied by a larger waist circumference, researchers say.

Rather than using BMI alone, they suggest considering waist circumference, muscle mass, body composition and a person's overall health.

A person's Body Mass Index (BMI) may not tell the full story about their risk of dying in older age, with new research suggesting waist circumference can identify risks that a normal BMI misses.

The study of 6,905 adults in the United States aged 65 and over found that being overweight was associated with a lower mortality hazard than having a normal BMI, particularly among men.

But a larger waist circumference was associated with a higher mortality hazard in both men and women.

The researchers say the findings do not mean obesity is protective. Instead, they highlight the limitations of using BMI as the sole indicator of a person's health.

BMI, or body mass index, is a measure calculated from a person's height and weight. It is commonly used to classify people as underweight, normal weight, overweight or obese, but it does not distinguish between muscle and fat.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"BMI and waist circumference provide complementary information about health risk in older adults," co-author Dr Bryan Blissmer from the University of Rhode Island said.

"Our findings suggest that considering both measures together, rather than relying on BMI alone, may improve mortality risk assessment and support more informed clinical decision-making."

What did the study consider?

In the study, a BMI below 18.5 was considered underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 was considered normal weight, 25 to 29.9 was considered overweight, and 30 or above was considered obese.

Obesity was divided into three classes: Class I, BMI 30 to 34.9; Class II, 35 to 39.9; and Class III, 40 or above.

However, for their analysis, the researchers combined Class I and Class II into a single category.

The researchers analysed 14 years of data from the US National Health and Aging Trends Study, following 6,905 people from 2011 to 2024.

They used a statistical measure called a hazard ratio to compare the likelihood of death occurring over the follow-up period between different groups.

A hazard ratio of 1 indicates no difference from the comparison group. A value below 1 indicates a lower hazard of death, while a value above 1 indicates a higher hazard.

For example, a hazard ratio of 0.5 represents roughly half the mortality hazard of the comparison group, while a ratio of 2 represents roughly twice the hazard.

What were the results for men and women?

The study found important differences between men and women, particularly in the relationship between BMI and mortality.

Among men, being overweight was associated with a 46 per cent lower mortality hazard than having a normal BMI. Men with Class I or II obesity also had a lower mortality hazard, at 51 per cent lower than men in the normal BMI range.

The pattern was weaker among women. Overweight women had a 27 per cent lower mortality hazard than women with a normal BMI. The lower hazard observed among women with Class I or II obesity was not statistically significant, suggesting it may have been due to chance.

READ MORE Can this small patch really help you lose weight and live a healthier life?

Waist circumference showed a much more consistent pattern. A waist circumference above 40 inches (102 centimetres) for men or 35 inches (89 centimetres) for women was associated with a 24 per cent higher mortality hazard in both sexes, independent of BMI.

The researchers also found that a normal BMI could mask higher risk. Men with a normal BMI but a high waist circumference had a 33 per cent higher mortality hazard, while women had a 23 per cent higher hazard.

Being underweight was also associated with almost twice the mortality hazard in both men and women.

Overall, the association between higher BMI and lower mortality was stronger in men, whereas the relationship between larger waist circumference and higher mortality was similar in both sexes.

Understanding the 'obesity paradox'

Associate professor David Scott from Deakin University's Institute for Physical Activity said that measuring health solely by BMI creates an "obesity paradox".

"It demonstrates the 'obesity paradox': the finding that in older adults and some populations with chronic health conditions, higher body mass indexes, even in the overweight or obese range, can protect against mortality," he said.

BMI cannot distinguish between muscle and fat, nor can it show where fat is stored.

"Because BMI does not distinguish between fat and lean mass, the 'obesity paradox' may be explained by the fact that some people classified as overweight or obese have high amounts of lean mass and relatively low amounts of fat mass, while others who appear to be a healthy weight may actually have a high body fat percentage," Scott added.

The researchers argue that waist circumference can provide important additional information because fat stored around the abdomen is associated with metabolic and cardiovascular problems.

The researchers say the findings support a broader approach to assessing health in older adults.

Rather than relying on BMI alone, they suggest considering waist circumference, muscle mass, body composition and a person's overall health.

For older adults, the study's central message is that a "normal" or "healthy" BMI does not necessarily indicate low health risk, particularly when accompanied by a larger waist circumference.

title: Can Australia rebuild social cohesion? Inquiry hears calls for change
text:
in brief Over four days, commissioner Virginia Bell heard concerns about social cohesion and antisemitism.

The commission is in its 9th and final block of hearings.

Experts, advocates and community leaders are calling for stronger social cohesion and action on antisemitism, telling an inquiry "we need to break the cycle".

Over four days of hearings this week, commissioner Virginia Bell heard concerns about declining satisfaction with democracy, social media polarisation, racism, self-censorship and the breakdown of relationships between religious and cultural communities.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion also heard proposals for stronger education about Jewish Australians, better recognition of migrants’ qualifications and more effective approaches to tackling prejudice.

But the hearings also exposed difficult questions about what social cohesion should mean, including how Australia can combat discrimination without silencing debate.

The royal commission, launched in response to the December 2025 Bondi terror attack, is in its ninth and final block of hearings, with its final report due in December.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Here are the key takeaways from the week.

Questions about democracy

Professors Nicholas Biddle and Matthew Gray, both from the Australian National University, fronted the royal commission on Monday, speaking to reporters about democratic attitudes in Australia and responses about declining satisfaction with democracy.

Their June report found that satisfaction with democracy fell to its lowest level since January 2023, while principled support for democracy increased. Professor Gray said multiple factors could be at play, including social media undermining support for democracy.

"We conclude that efforts to counter antisemitism will be limited unless they also address the platforms through which distrust, polarisation and extremist narratives circulate," Gray told the commission.

He argued targeted interventions, particularly for young Australians with low educational attainment and low levels of principled democratic support, would be more effective than universal attempts to counter antisemitism.

"Because trust in core institutions is closely associated with democratic commitment, consideration should be given to how government agencies, education systems and public communications practices could be made more transparent, accountable and credible, particularly in communities experiencing disadvantage," Gray said.

Ahmed Hegazi, a strategic adviser, and his friend Joel Lazar, the chief executive of the Jewish Climate Network, also expressed concern about polarisation and emphasised the importance of cross-cultural communication.

"Humans who know their neighbours don't feel they are threats and they don't fear them, they feel connected to them," Hegazi said. "We need to break the cycle."

"There's basically no alternative to trying new things even if they're hard … as fathers of young children, we know important things are always hard," Lazar said.

Skills recognition proposed to ease tensions

Australian businessman, David Gonski told the inquiry his 24-member Antisemitism Education Taskforce was considering a proposal to improve recognition of migrants' skills and address community tensions.

Many skilled migrants were underemployed because their previous qualifications were not recognised.

"This, (a member) put to us, creates some tension and concern both within them and the people that they live with, and so on," he said on Tuesday.

"He felt that we could find a twofold solution: a solution that allowed us to have more skilled workers, and ... that would take away some of the aggravation that comes for these people."

Gonski said "there was merit" in considering the proposal but the task force had not reached a final decision. He stressed he was not suggesting further migration, but broader permissions for migrants to practice in their fields.

Gonski was appointed to lead the antisemitism education task force in December 2025 and previously filed the Gonski report on Australian education funding.

He also recommended broader education about Jewish contributions to Australia.

"We are hopeful that (the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority) will now look more broadly at not just Holocaust studies, but also more generally the contribution of the Jews and indeed the Jewish faith," he said.

"There's a lot of contribution by Jews to Australia, to the history of Australia."

Orthodox Rabbi Zalman Kastel suggested educators address specific prejudices in youth's education.

"Telling people a general message of don't be racist, doesn't cut it," he said.

Monash University lecturers Farid Zaid and Daniel Heller said students and staff had become afraid to address difficult topics, with many students struggling to hear different views.

"We both saw conversations in the classroom play out along really rigid lines," Zaid said.

"I was deeply surprised by my students' inability to distinguish discomfort in the classroom ... and distressed."

Most students and academics adopted self-censorship for fear of social media censure or official complaints. Others were inclined to, in Said and Heller's terms, "perform certainty"; project a sense of virtue over others.

"We know what's virtuous, what's moral, what's right; and anyone who disagrees is, in one way or another, morally reprehensible," Heller said.

The pair run Brave Conversations Project workshops teaching students and teachers how to stay in the room when discussions become difficult.

Terror attacks deepen Jewish-Muslim division

Faith Communities Council of Victoria's Sandy Kouroupidis said interaction between Jewish and Muslim communities had stopped altogether following the Bondi massacre on 14 December 2025, and the attack on Israel by Hamas militants on 7 October 2023.

The October 7 attacks by Hamas killed 1,200 people and resulted in 250 people being taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 70,000 people and been labeled a genocide by a United Nations commission, which the Israeli government disputes.

READ MORE Australia facing unprecedented levels of online hate speech, antisemitism inquiry told

"We have two vice chairs; one of them is the chair of the Islamic Council of Victoria and the other one is the chair of the Jewish Community Council of Victoria," he said.

"It has been very, very challenging to get those two communities in the same room."

Jewish people had stopped attending interfaith events, while schools stopped visiting Muslim and Christian institutes.

"A lot of the Jewish schools simply don't feel safe," he said.

Social cohesion must not hide racism

Race Discrimination Commissioner Giridharan Sivaraman warned that social cohesion can camouflage racial discrimination.

"Stop talking about racism because you're disrupting the social cohesion," Sivaraman said he was told by a senior government official.

He said social cohesion policies could resemble those used to justify racial assimilation and cause distrust.

"If it's obscuring, then it's not actually solving the systemic or structural problem that you need to fix," he told the inquiry.

"If your experience of policies or laws or programs under the term social cohesion are ones where you're excluded ... or you have to assimilate ... you won't trust the institutions you're engaging with."

Mourners place flowers at a memorial at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Saturday, December 20, 2025. Australia is in mourning after gunmen opened fire on Bondi Beach, killing 15 people in an attack designed to target the Jewish community. (AAP Image/Bianca De Marchi) NO ARCHIVING Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

Sivaraman also said reports of antisemitism, particularly in workplaces, had risen sharply since the October 7 attacks on Israel.

"Workplaces ended up being a really consistent theme that came up as an area where people felt disadvantaged," Sivaraman said.

"(They felt) they couldn't express their identity, felt they were in danger of losing their job, felt the inquiry also heard conflicting views over where legitimate criticism of Zionism ends and antisemitism begins."

READ MORE Five key takeaways from the first week of antisemitism royal commission hearings

Separately, Rita Jabri Markwell, principal policy adviser to the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network, argued Zionism should be treated as a political ideology rather than a protected characteristic.

"It's not a race or religion," she said.

Jewish witnesses had described Zionism as inseparable from their religious and cultural identity. Markwell argued courts had increasingly taken her view and warned that treating Zionism as protected risked excluding Jewish Australians who rejected the ideology.

"The mere fact that there is a portion of Jewish people who do not accept that it is central to their identity indicates that it is an ideology," she said.

title: This Liberal MP took a journey from northern China — heading somewhere few Australians dare visit
text:
Ted O'Brien's path to Parliament has taken him where few Australians, and indeed Westerners, have gone before: North Korea’s capital, Pyongyang.

Before becoming an MP, the Opposition foreign affairs spokesperson worked across Asia.

He was living in Beijing with his wife Sophia, who was working for the International Crisis Group, when the opportunity came to join a small group of fifteen to visit the authoritarian state in 2010.

The occasion was the 65th anniversary of the ruling Workers' Party — at a time when Kim Jong-il’s reign was waning, and the transition was underway to son Kim Jong-Un.

"The North Koreans choreographed everything, but you can't hide everything," he told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He spent most of the visit in the North Korean capital, arriving by air and leaving by train through northern China.

The Australian government now lists North Korea in the "do not travel" category on its official Smartraveller advice portal.

The access O'Brien had to the secretive nation is rare.

"You'd hop in a bus, you'd go to a school and you'd meet a few parents and school kids. Then you'd go to a small shopping strip, and you'd realise the kids from the school, the same kids at the shopping strip."

Ted O'Brien visited North Korea with a small group of fifteen in 2010. Source: SBS News / Supplied

"It'd be like this theatre that would follow us around trying to portray a very different North Korea."

One encounter with reality came, perhaps ironically, at the sprawling Kumsusan Palace of the Sun, where the state’s leaders are buried, and it serves as the sacred centre of the North Korean mythos.

O’Brien says the "organisers muddled things up" and his tour ended up sharing a room with a group of workers, the best in each of their factories, given the coveted opportunity to pay their respects.

"This was the moment of their life … wearing their best possible, albeit all the same uniform," O'Brien recounts.

READ MORE Trump and Kim's renewed bromance stirs new and old threats for Australia

"That is where you saw their real poverty, and it sounds crude to say it, but you could smell the poverty, you could see the poverty, the eyes completely focusing down.

"And this is people's most happy day in their life. That will always stay with me of just a human reminder of what an authoritarian regime can mean."

After working across Asia, including Taiwan and China, O’Brien was elected to the seat of Fairfax in 2016, and now the Coalition's foreign affairs spokesperson has been putting his "rusty" Mandarin skills to use, fronting Liberal Party messaging on Chinese language social media, and giving speeches in the language.

"I'm a big believer that there's nothing more important than national unity," he explains.

"I think national unity is a critical part of our national security. It is vitally important if we are to withstand coercion as a country.”

While describing English as Australia’s "primary language”, O'Brien says politicians also need to "respect the dignity of the individual”, claiming English as a "far harder" language to learn than Chinese.

"If an individual is still struggling to engage with our national language, well, let me engage with him or her in their language if we can, so they understand that once they become an Australian, they are absolutely part of our family as Aussies.”

The last Liberal Party review was scathing about the party’s struggles to engage with multicultural communities, identifying "the party's capacity to thoughtlessly offend groups, including the Chinese" as a "widespread problem", and singling out how Jane Hume’s remarks about "Chinese spies" were successfully weaponised by Labor in the final days of the campaign.

O’Brien argued his in-language approach was driven by a "genuine desire to ensure we have unity in Australia", saying he’s picked up on concerns among Chinese Australian voters about Beijing's ethnic unity laws.

"They need to know that their country is absolutely with them, that there's nothing more important than being an Australian."

Separately, O'Brien was partially successful in pressuring the government to amend updated foreign arrangements laws to force greater scrutiny of academics' independent research.

The Coalition had voiced concerns that a loophole in the laws allowed researchers to independently collaborate with institutions from so-called "rogue" states, without Commonwealth oversight.

"If it falls under the auspices of a university, then the Commonwealth knows about it. But if the professor decides to do it on his own without the university banner, the Commonwealth doesn't know about it. The risk is the same to the Australian people," he said.

This week, Foreign Minister Penny Wong intervened to shut down an ANU partnership with China’s Shandong University by 2027. It followed a Pentagon call to blacklist the institution over concerns about its research links with the Chinese state.

"What we have to have is risk-aware engagement; that's the approach we've taken, that's the approach we need," Wong said.

A young local family paid $3.92 million for a charming clinker brick house in Kew at auction on Saturday, beating a buyer’s agent in what the selling agent called one of the first competitive auctions he had seen in months. The five-bedroom home at 22 Ridgeway Avenue dates to about 1935 and retains its heritage character but has been updated and converted from a duplex into a family home with a gourmet kitchen, outdoor entertaining area, large windows and a landscaped garden. The property was one of 570 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 58 per cent from 365 reported results throughout the week, while 67 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Two parties competed for the Kew home, which had been listed with a price guide of $3.5 million to $3.8 million.

Already, the knives are being sharpened. Days after Harry and Meghan’s shock announcement of a UK return, the notorious British media is baying for blood. Here in the UK, as elsewhere, there is confusion over the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex after six years. Why take on this extraordinary pressure of moving back? Especially when there is little sign of any thaw in the hostility that they say drove them away? There is no apparent reconciliation with their family – King Charles was himself only informed of their return a few days ago. Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex meet people after viewing the floral tributes for the late Queen Elizabeth II outside Windsor Castle, in 2022. AP Harry just lost a major case against the British tabloids and, along with six other high-profile claimants, must pay an eye-watering £9.54 million ($18.16 million) towards the Daily Mail publisher’s legal costs. Even Meghan’s new acting role in Netflix series The Gentleman seems less than certain, as reports say it has been withdrawn “due to a public backlash”.

Advertisement

The UK public are not clamouring for the couple’s return to the fold. Polling by YouGov for The Sunday Times found that 51 per cent would oppose the duke and duchess returning as full-time working royals. Sky News polling found that 44 per cent opposed their return. The Sun headlined with one readers’ reaction that it was a “publicity stunt”, and amid a cost of living crisis 80 per cent of the tabloid’s readers say the Sussexes should fund their own security. Brits are, at best, divided by their return. As a British-born journalist who has written for the UK tabloid Harry sued – The Sun – and other Murdoch titles, I should be Harry’s bête noire. Yet I admire him. Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Harry and Meghan, at the Royal Children’s Hospital on a recent visit to Australia. The Age Harry impressively fought journalistic bullies, demonstrating in previous successful court cases that British tabloids were willing to drive people to paranoia through their inappropriate surveillance. The prince and his wife were two of the few people who had the money, profile and determination to challenge such unethical behaviour. Good for them. I don’t blame them for demanding privacy, then selling memoirs and Netflix shows telling their story on their own terms and making money for their own children. To me, they got the last laugh.

Advertisement

Except there’s nothing funny about how short our memories are. Have we learnt nothing from Diana’s death, The Leveson Inquiry into phone hacking or the tragedy of the bullying of Charlotte Dawson? Another perspective Opinion

Royal family It’s obvious what’s behind Harry and Meghan’s return to Blighty. It’s not to reunite with Will and Kate Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist Tabloid hounding and spiteful reporting ruins lives – and kills women. The pen is always mightier than the sword. Yet the UK tabloids remain blood-stained red tops. Have we forgotten Earl Spencer’s eulogy about his sister? “I always believed the press would kill her in the end… [they] have blood on their hands.” Can anyone truly blame Harry for fighting against such dark history being repeated with his wife? Have we forgotten, also, that the 2012 Leveson Inquiry, following the News International phone hacking scandal, found a UK press culture that ignored its own ethical code in the pursuit of stories through covert surveillance?

Advertisement

The less cynical view for the Sussex’s surprise UK return is one you won’t read much now the couple’s name is dirt on Fleet Street. They’re returning, perhaps, because they want the best life for their kids – educationally, financially and familially. The fantastic Invictus Games for wounded soldiers, founded by Harry, will be in Birmingham next year. And there’s a non-financial reason to ask for state-funded security: In Britain, private security staff cannot lawfully carry guns, pepper spray, batons or tasers, no matter what you pay them. Terrorist group al-Qaeda and other extremists have already threatened Harry, who twice served in Afghanistan, with murder. And how much bile will be stirred before Meghan’s life, too, is endangered via incitement to hatred? Especially at a time of rising British nationalism and violent jingoism. And it isn’t just the tabloids who pile on. Writing for The Times this weekend, columnist Camilla Long claimed the couple were tearing up their principles to “come back to a country they hate,” due to a “resentment and disappointment at the snobbery and structural racism that they think defines Britain”. She argues Harry wants to “destroy the monarchy” and that Meghan is “the worst actress that ever lived”.

Exclusive Eating outComing soon A St Kilda dining icon will soon get a fresh start from a rising restaurant star “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us.” Superstar chef Ellie Bouhadana, formerly of Hope St Radio, will open her first restaurant in a Barkly Street site that comes with 28 years of memories. Dani Valent August 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a successful summer seafood pop-up at Stokehouse’s beachfront kiosk in St Kilda, and recent months cooking and eating her way around Morocco, Italy and the Netherlands, ex-Hope St Radio chef Ellie Bouhadana is launching her own restaurant. Dafina Seaside Grill will open in the storied Claypots site in St Kilda in early 2027, adding extra verve to an exciting time for the suburb, with Andrew McConnell’s Trader House taking over Stokehouse in spring and new developments happening on down-at-heel Fitzroy Street. Chef Ellie Bouhadana and husband Rapha Tamir will open Dafina Seaside Grill in the former Claypots site. Simon Schluter “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us,” says Bouhadana, who lives locally and is working alongside husband Rapha Tamir. “My parents brought me to Acland Street when I was a kid, for ice-cream, cakes and Luna Park. We came to Claypots, too. We couldn’t let it be gutted, maybe turned into a KFC.” Tamir’s grandparents came for regular Friday spaghetti marinara lunches and he remembers long meals under the courtyard’s bougainvillea. “It felt celebratory, with a casual, affordable approach to seafood,” he says.

Advertisement

1 / 3 The enormous octopus that once hung from Claypots’ ceiling. Erin Slattery 2 / 3 The bar of Claypots in January 2007, with seahorse door handles visible (right). Erin Slattery 3 / 3 Ellie Bouhadana and Rapha Tamir with the quirky Claypots doors. Simon Schluter Previous Slide Next Slide Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Renan Goksin opened Claypots in 1998, serving gumbos, chilli crab and simple grills. The atmosphere was bohemian, musical and charmingly chaotic. Neelam Sami took over in 2016 and Claypots remained a grungy slice of old-time St Kilda until it closed in February. Goksin has pointed out special features to the restaurant’s new custodians, who will retain some in their new fit-out. “He told me the bar is made from stolen pieces of the old St Kilda pier, so that’s non-negotiable,” says Tamir. Canvas sails are suspended from rope pulleys as de facto air-conditioning. Carved seahorses double as door handles. Walls are stuck with faux Sumerian tablets etched with cuneiform (the world’s oldest-known writing system), clustered around one that is apparently real. An enormous pressed tin octopus hangs from the ceiling – a head-scraping hazard, but also an icon. “We like the quirks and the energy but we’ll do our own thing,” says Tamir. “It’s going to be Ellie’s food, but we do feel attracted to St Kilda institutions and the Jewish immigrant story here.”

Advertisement

It will be the debut restaurant of chef Ellie Bouhadana (right), in partnership with Rapha Tamir. Simon Schluter Dafina is named for a Sephardi Jewish slow-cooked meat-and-grain dish that speaks to Bouhadana’s Jewish Moroccan heritage. “It’s a claypot cooked overnight in the communal fire, in the embers of the dying coals,” she says. In Jewish culture, foods are often slowly cooked on Friday night’s cooling fire, ready for the Sabbath when cooking is not allowed. “We’ll also do Moroccan-style brochette [kebabs], whole fish with cumin and garlic, lamb chops, dips and salad, lots of oil and vinegar, food for swiping with fresh-baked flatbreads.” Related Article How to make one of Melbourne’s favourite focaccias at home Bouhadana first came to attention for her lockdown pop-ups, including pasta parties and sandwiches sold from her driveway. She was the first chef at Collingwood wine-slash-listening bar Hope St Radio in 2021, and took the restaurant to a hat in the 2023 Age Good Food Guide. She left in 2024 and released her cookbook, Ellie’s Table, continuing with events and catering in Australia and overseas.

Advertisement

“I’ve been nervous to commit to a site,” she says. “But what I love about pop-ups is working with interesting people who become friends as we explore each other’s food and hosting style. It’s exciting to think about sharing my own hospitality. There’s a renewal in St Kilda, and we’re excited to put down roots and be part of that.” Dafina Seaside Grill opens early 2027 at 213 Barkly Street, St Kilda.

The Australian sharemarket has advanced at the open on the back of a positive lead from Wall Street, while National Australia Bank chief Andrew Irvine has warned the Australian economy risks being stuck in a “trap” of low economic growth because of its poor performance on productivity. The Australian sharemarket rose 23 points or 0.3 per cent, to 9087.9 in early trade. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.64¢. Markets are waiting for a breakthrough in the Middle East. AP Banking stocks retreated at the open, with Commonwealth Bank down 1.7 per cent and National Australia Bank losing 0.7 per cent. ANZ fell 0.9 per cent and Westpac shed 0.5 per cent. NAB boss Irvine, who has previously warned that economic conditions for Australia could be “as good as it gets”, said on Monday the risk now was one of poor long-term economic performance thanks to much weaker productivity growth than other advanced economies. “The risk now is not that we are at the peak of the mountain – it’s that we slide down the other side, stuck in a low-productivity, low-growth trap that’s been slowly strangling Australia for decades,” Irvine said.

Related Article Analysis

Home loans ‘Frighteningly easy’: How fake AI payslips fuel mortgage fraud “Without urgent action, we’ll be locked in a slow lane – sitting in the rearview mirror of other advanced economies surging past us.” Mining stocks advanced on the back of strengthening commodities prices, with the iron ore giants leading the way. BHP jumped 3.1 per cent, Fortescue rose 1.8 per cent and Rio Tinto advanced 1.2 per cent in early trade. Gold stocks had more muted gains, with Northern Star edging up 0.1 per cent and Evolution Mining adding 0.4 per cent. Drinks giant Endeavour Group slid 5.9 per cent after revealing flat group sales, declining earnings and net profits, gross margins and reduced dividends. Group sales lifted just 1.3 per cent to $12.2 billion for the 2026 financial year, but underlying earnings and net profits declined 8.7 per cent and 14.8 per cent respectively. Dan Murphy’s and BWS sales rose just 1 per cent to $9.8 billion over the year as growth in the retail division lagged its hotels business, which gained 4.2 per cent to $2.2 billion.

The retail business’ underlying gross profits declined 86 basis points as it leant more heavily into promotions to make sales. Meanwhile, the hotels business benefited from people gathering for the FIFA World Cup and greater investment in pub refurbishments and poker machines. Energy stocks retreated, oil sliding lower in early Asian trade ahead of US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s press conference detailing a plan to economically isolate Iran. Brent, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to $US93.05 a barrel while US oil lost 1.6 per cent to $US85.71. Technology stocks are mixed, with WiseTech adding 1.6 per cent, Xero up 2.1 per cent and Technology One rising 2 per cent, but Megaport lost 2.3 per cent and NEXTDC fell 1.3 per cent. On Friday, the S&P 500 rose 0.4 per cent for just its second gain in the six days since setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones jumped 517 points, or 1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.4 per cent. After soaring through the northern summer and then hesitating following this week’s surprise move by the US Treasury Department to repurchase more US government bonds, yields climbed further on Friday.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.73 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Thursday. It’s back above its level from before the Treasury market made its move, which analysts said at the time was likely to have only a temporary effect. The 30-year Treasury yield, which the Fed is also targeting with its bond repurchases, also rose and is near its highest level since 2007. Contributing to Friday’s gains for bond yields was continued uncertainty about when the US-Israeli war on Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. That caused oil prices to rise, which affects Treasury yields because they increase worries about inflation. Related Article Energy Labor’s plan to reserve more domestic gas stirs hopes of a revival Besides inflation, concerns about the fast-rising debt for the US government have also been sending yields upward. Higher yields can slow the economy and undercut prices for all kinds of investments. One of the biggest beneficiaries of Bessent’s move to try to get longer-term yields lower is bitcoin. Cryptocurrencies often rise when interest rates are lower and more money is flowing through the financial system. Hopes for legislation in Washington to help the crypto industry have also helped it.

The Treasury Department’s buyback announcement has helped weaken the US dollar’s value against other currencies, which tends to give gold’s price a boost. That helped drive stocks of miners higher. KPMG chief executive John Sams said 27 partners and 360 employees will be cut this week as the scandalised firm deals with a significant decline in its consulting business and the impending loss of audit work following the whistleblower scandal. “After careful consideration, we have made the difficult decision to reduce our workforce and restructure parts of the firm. Thomas Wielecki Sams informed KPMG’s 9,000 employees in an all-staff call at 10.30 this morning. The KPMG statement included references to its 2026 financial results which reported that revenue declined slightly to $2.26 billion due to a 17 per cent plunge in its largest business, consulting, which is bearing the brunt of these cuts. KPMG has been in turmoil since a whistleblower revealed partners of the firm had accessed confidential client data to win new business, a serious breach of trust.

The fallout from the scandal is also starting to impact on its business. “We also recognise the challenges created by our own failings, and the work we must continue to do to rebuild trust,” Sams said. “We need to be clear about the outlook. We expect difficult market conditions to continue in FY27 (financial year) and beyond.” KPMG partners are already feeling the impact with the firm reporting that average equity partner pay dropped 13 per cent last year. It adds to a tough environment for all of the consulting giants which have been cutting staff this year. “Economic growth is expected to remain subdued until at least 2028, affecting client investment and extending decision-making timeframes. The professional services sector is also changing rapidly as client expectations evolve, AI reshapes the way services are delivered and government spending on consultants remains lower,” Sams said. “While these conditions are likely to persist, we remain focused on what we can control. A century-old house with shagpile carpet and mustard-coloured lino that has never changed hands has now sold for a reserve-smashing $3.225 million. Perched on an 899-square-metre parcel with city views, the unrenovated three-bedroom house at 74 Agnes Street in Auchenflower was described as one of the last of its kind. Beneath its peeling mid-century wallpaper, it offered a prime piece of land with three-street frontage and a subdivision opportunity that could see it split into two corner lots in what is now Brisbane’s third-most expensive suburb. Seven buyers – representing a mix of developers and owner-occupiers – registered for the Saturday auction and six bid. A Redcliffe family kicked off bidding at $2.1 million, sparking a developer to quickly counter with $2.52 million.

Advertisement

“We had a few buyers hesitating after that,” said selling agent Josh Brown, of Ray White Collective. “That brought the price pretty close to the reserve, so we paused and then called it on the market.” The three-bedroom house at 74 Agnes Street is perched on an 899-square-metre parcel with city views. Ray White It sparked a flurry of more than 100 rises ranging between $500 and $25,000, including one eyebrow-raising bid of $2,842,368.74. Yet even that precise rise didn’t slow momentum. At $3.225 million the hammer dropped and a local family claimed the keys.

Advertisement

“They were so happy,” Brown said. “It’s a pretty unique house with a northern aspect on a big allotment surrounded by beautiful homes. The carpet and wallpaper could do with an update but didn’t stymie interest in the house. Ray White “And it’s untouched … it was owned by the same family for 100 years. There are not many homes like this left here.” The auction came weeks after Auchenflower muscled its way into Brisbane’s top-three priciest suburbs. Domain’s June House Price Report showed house medians skyrocketed 26.1 per cent in 12 months to $2.175 million.

While the pocket’s pulling power underpinned the result, Brown said buyer confidence had also crept back. The home was one of 153 scheduled auctions across south-east Queensland. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 20 per cent from 94 reported results, with 16 homes withdrawn. In Hawthorne, a two-bedroom, one-bathroom townhouse sold for $1.02 million after three active bidders battled for the keys. A woman who had sold her place in Newstead six months earlier, and was living with a friend, claimed the prize. Perched on a 169-square-metre lot in a complex of six, the townhouse at 2/71 Miles Street features a balcony, yard and a recently upgraded bathroom. It last sold two years ago for $826,000.

Advertisement

Seven bidders registered and three competed after the auction opened at $900,000. After an early pause, a vendor bid of $1 million sparked a few more rises until it sold. Selling agent Eliza Schultz, of Place Bulimba, said the price was a record for the complex and highlighted the strong buyer competition at that price point. “This was one of the strongest auctions we’ve had in a while … we had really good engagement from day one,” she said. “Townhouses are performing very well at the moment, especially in blue chip areas like Hawthorne.”

Advertisement

Schultz said the home attracted single couples, first-home buyers, upsizers and a few investors, adding that the owner’s pre-auction prep added to the strong interest. “He did everything we recommended … including a fresh lick of paint, updating the carpet and a basic bathroom renovation,” she said. “It looked flawless. It cost him probably $25,000 to $30,000 but it meant any buyers coming through knew there was nothing to do.” In Ascot, an iconic family estate built in the ’90s sold under the hammer for $5.25 million to a local buyer who only set foot in the home just 24 hours beforehand. It was the highest auction sale price in south-east Queensland at the weekend.

Advertisement

The six-bedroom, three-bathroom home – called Kynuna – sits on an 810-square-metre block at 7 Lonsdale Street and features manicured gardens, a fireplace and a media room. Three registered buyers – two locals and one remote – bid after the auction opened at $4 million. The price climbed to $5.2 million, where the ultimate buyer offered a final rise to clinch the prize. Ray White Ascot’s Damon Warat – who co-sold the home with Nick Roche – said the result belied the property’s prime location in one of the suburb’s best streets near “booming infrastructure”. “It’s so close to Racecourse Road, where hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent,” he said.

“While A-grade real estate is always sought after, larger bigger properties are getting more demand than smaller ones right now and that’s because the only tax benefits that remain are in the primary residence.” This is the third time the home has changed hands in three years, selling in July 2024 for $4.24 million. PRD Nationwide chief economist Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo said while Brisbane’s market was stabilising, the weekend’s low clearance rate reflected the loss of investors. “If investors want to access negative gearing they need to buy new, and you can’t auction something that doesn’t exist yet,” she said. “And that has limited investor demand in the auction market. “But property demand is still high and we’re still tracking around 4.8 per cent median house price growth in Brisbane.”

title: ‘Scroungers’ or worth a second chance: What Londoners really think of Harry and Meghan

Analysis WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘Scroungers’ or worth a second chance: What Londoners really think of Harry and Meghan David Crowe Updated August 24, 2026 — 10:25am ,first published August 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
