London: The Duke of Sussex is waiting for me when I alight from Waterloo Station and walk along busy streets on a sunny afternoon as people head out for drinks and dinner. Before I get to the pub and its popular beer garden, however, I have work to do. I slow down so I can ask people what they think about Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, making an imminent return to Britain. And I find Londoners have as many opinions about the royal family as they have bus routes. Empathy can be hard to find on the streets of London, but at least there’s some in the beer garden of the Duke of Sussex. Alamy Stock Photo “I think they’re welcome – it would be better for everyone if they reunited as a family,” says Karl, a man in his 30s who is rushing for a train.

Advertisement

“They should stay away,” says a woman in her 50s. “It’s an irrelevance,” says Benedict, a communications professional. “The royal family is an ancient hangover of a corrupt society.” Loading Big questions surround the royal couple’s return with their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. The children are due to start at a British school as soon as next week, the beginning of the school year, and the family are said to be moving to a private residence just outside London. The British press is full of speculation about whether the government will assign security to the family; when Meghan will resume her acting career; whether King Charles will welcome them home; and whether Harry can reconcile with his brother, William, the Prince of Wales.

Advertisement

Even those who have a soft spot for Harry – the actual Duke of Sussex, of course – wonder why he is coming back after speaking out against the royal family during his six years in California. “I don’t mind Harry. I think he’ll be fine,” says Helen McMahon, a doctor who is out for the day with her two young children. “But I think they’ve become pretty unpopular because nobody likes Meghan because they think she’s a gold digger. Doctor Helen McMahon believes the royal family is now a waste of money. David Crowe “And they’ve tried to monetise everything and televise everything. So, I wonder whether they can just change their minds that easily and return.” McMahon believes the royal family is now a waste of money, although she liked the late Queen Elizabeth II. Here in central London, it is not hard to find others who feel the same way.

Advertisement

“I think they’re scroungers,” says Martin, a middle-aged salesman. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? “I think the media feeds them. They feed the media. They can all eff off. They cost the country too much. I have no interest in them. “All the royal family should be taken off somewhere. Buckingham Palace can be turned into a nice youth hostel or a nice homeless hostel.” It is about two months since King Charles disclosed accounts showing the royal family cost taxpayers £132 million ($250 million) last year. The latest polling shows 64 per cent of British voters believe the UK should keep its monarchy, but the cost of the institution is clearly a concern on the streets near Waterloo Station.

Advertisement

David Ashcroft, a shipping industry worker, says Harry and Meghan can do as they wish as long as they pay their own way. “They’ve let themselves down, I think, by behaving like children,” he says. Shipping industry worker David Ashcroft says Harry and Meghan can do as they wish as long as they pay their own way. David Crowe “You have to reap what you sow. Harry is estranged from his brother, and I think he’s an embarrassment, really, and he should be ashamed of himself for not having more self-control.” Ashcroft has not read the prince’s memoir, Spare, but he has seen enough about the book to feel that Harry has only himself to blame for his rift with his family.

Advertisement

“One of the great British characteristics is if you have a problem, you don’t talk about it,” he says. Related Article Analysis

Royal family For Harry and Meghan, going home might just reopen old family wounds “People think everything needs to be spoken about these days. It doesn’t. It doesn’t get better when you share it, sometimes. “So I think he should have kept it all to himself, been a professional about it and then dealt with it himself.” Who should pay for security for the family when Harry and Meghan arrive on British soil?

Advertisement

“They should,” Ashcroft says. Others say the same here on Baylis Road in the Borough of Lambeth, south of the Thames. I am only a short walk from the street where William Blake, artist and poet, railed against the monarchy two centuries ago. “I don’t think they should get back their royal contingent of security,” says Max Bateman, an airport worker in his 30s. “They decided to step away from that. If they don’t want to be part of the royal family, then they don’t get the perks of being in the royal family.” Could Harry and Meghan return to their old royal duties in some way? There is not a lot of sympathy for them on this front. “I think it’s a one-way decision,” Bateman says. “They stepped away. If you don’t want to be in the limelight, stay out of the limelight.” Bella Paksi, a university student about to turn 20, also thinks security should be up to the family, not the state.

Advertisement

“They should be on their own. They’ve got enough money,” she says. “There shouldn’t be our tax money going towards that.” While others believe the monarchy has outlived its usefulness, Paksi says there is still support for the royal family among the young. Uni student Bella Paksi thinks security should be up to the family, not the state. David Crowe “I think that it does bring a net positive, and also it means holding on to what historical roots England does have,” she says. “So I think that keeping the royal family is a good thing for that reason.”

Advertisement

I walk to the pub knowing, even more surely than I did before, that Harry and Meghan will struggle to find any support from the British public when they return. A YouGov survey last month found 58 per cent had a negative view of Harry; 65 per cent had a negative view of Meghan. Then I’m stopped by a council street sweeper, working in bright orange overalls, who wants to know why I’ve been asking people so many questions. Prudence has a kind heart. She tells me it would be good for Harry and Meghan to be reconciled with the family. ‘They stepped away. If you don’t want to be in the limelight, stay out of the limelight.’ Max Bateman, an airport worker in his 30s “The children should be able to see their cousins,” she says. But what about all the things Harry has said about his father, his brother and the rest of the family? “They should give him a second chance.” And, once I get to the pub, I meet Sion, 30, who is sipping a white wine with a friend in the beer garden.

Advertisement

“I just wish them the best,” she says. “I actually don’t have any negative feelings about them at all. I think everyone’s a bit mean about them, to be honest. I’ve moved abroad before and come back. I don’t think it’s that deep, is it?” Unlike others, Sion has no problem with the government arranging security for Harry and his family. “He didn’t ask to be born into that life where you need security,” she says. “If I was being harassed by a stalker, I’d hope that the police and whatnot would look after me.

“I kind of feel sorry for anyone who’s famous. I would hate it. So, I think maybe I have a bit more empathy for them.” Empathy can be hard to find on the streets of London, but at least there’s some in the beer garden of the Duke of Sussex. title: Scandal-hit KPMG rakes in billions, slashes jobs
text:
A major consultancy firm that has been under fire for practices in its audit business will cut its local workforce after being suspended from applying for government contracts.

KPMG, which is one of the top four firms behind Deloitte, PwC and EY, on Monday revealed its annual revenue fell one per cent to $2.5 billion in fiscal 2026.

It also warned the outlook for the new year remained difficult.

"We expect difficult market conditions to continue in financial year 2027 and beyond," new chief executive John Sams said.

KPMG Australia CEO John Sams warned of continuing difficult market conditions. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS)

A continuation of soft market conditions in 2025/26, as well as a continued reduction in the use of consultants by governments, resulted in a 16.9 per cent decrease in revenue for the consulting business.

However, revenue for its audit and assurance and tax and legal arms rose 11 per cent and 10.9 per cent, respectively.

After reviewing its costs and workforce and the impact of the firm's conduct and whistleblower matters, it will cut jobs by five per cent.

The reduction will mostly hit its consulting and business services arm and take out 27 partners and around 360 employees.

"This result reflects the resilience of our business and, above all, the commitment of our people in a very challenging year," Mr Sams said on Monday.

"We will continue to monitor performance closely, act when needed and consider carefully how the firm needs to be set up for the future."

But while revenue was below its expectations, four out of its five businesses grew, Mr Sams noted.

However, its partners won't escape the revenue dip, with average equity partner remuneration falling by 13 per cent on the prior year.

KPMG has been banned from applying for federal government contracts until at least the end of September, when the finance department expects to have completed its own review of its conduct.

KPMG executives appeared at a parliamentary inquiry earlier this month. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS)

A number of state governments have also put KPMG on ice.

The firm has been engulfed by an audit leak scandal since it was grilled by a federal government parliamentary committee hearing in June.

It was revealed some executives had misused confidential board papers to win new audit contracts and mistreated a whistleblower who raised concerns.

The firm has also been referred to the National Anti-Corruption Commission by committee member and Greens senator Barbara Pocock.

The scandal has claimed numerous executives, including its former chief executive Andrew Yates and chair Martin Sheppard.

Mr Sams confirmed several internal and external reviews of the firm will be completed in the coming months.

"Their findings will inform the next phase of our action plan and help ensure we take all necessary action," he said.

"We know there is more to do."

KPMG has 297 active federal contracts worth $653 million.

title: The AFL finals haven’t changed in 25 years, until now. What is the wildcard round?
text:
This weekend, the AFL will unveil a first: a "wildcard round".

This round involves two matches to kick off the finals series, in the first change to the league's finals format in 25 years.

On Friday, the Western Bulldogs will host Collingwood in the first wildcard final, with Melbourne then taking on Carlton on Saturday night.

But why was this brought in, how will it work, and how have the league's finals series evolved over time?

How the wildcard round works

In recent years the top eight teams have had a week off between the regular season and the start of the finals.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

However, this year only the top six teams get a week off. The teams ranked seven to ten will play in the wildcard round: seventh will play tenth and eighth will play ninth.

The two winners will continue on to the next finals game, with the two losers eliminated.

The wildcard concept, sometimes called a "play-in tournament", has been a fixture of popular sports leagues such as the United States' Major League Baseball and National Basketball Association for many years.

It was introduced to Australia's National Basketball League and Victorian Football League in 2023.

Initial reactions were mostly negative

When the AFL announced the changed finals format in November last year, it highlighted several key benefits for clubs, players and fans.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

These included greater reward for finishing in the top six, more teams making finals, and all top-eight teams hosting a home final.

The league also believed there would be more games of "consequence" towards the end of the season, while supporters would embrace an extra week of finals.

However, the announcement was met with negative responses from players, coaches, commentators and fans.

Critics described it as more unwanted Americanisation of Australian sport, and argued it may take attention away from the AFLW, which kicked off two weekends ago.

Many also believe the concept rewards mediocrity, as teams only have to finish in the top ten (out of 18 teams) to be in contention for the premiership.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

It was also labelled a cash grab by Geelong coach Chris Scott.

As the season progressed, more supported it

In recent weeks, as the wildcard round has got closer, fans and commentators began to express some more excitement about the concept, especially fans of teams that finished ninth and tenth (Collingwood and Carlton).

Having more teams from the lower part of the ladder still able to sneak into the finals when they previously would have been eliminated added to the interest.

There were concerns though that teams that were safely in the top ten, but could not make the top six, would rest large numbers of their best players in the week before the wildcard round to ensure they didn't get injured.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

This had the potential to reduce the quality of games in the final round of the regular season.

However, this did not occur, possibly due to the AFL sending clubs a memo warning them not to.

Not the first change to the finals format

The addition of a wildcard round is not the first change to the AFL finals.

Since the first AFL/VFL season in 1897, the finals have evolved from four teams (1901–71), to five (1972–90), six (1991–93), eight (1994–2025) and now ten teams.

The four-, six- and eight-team finals series have also had several different formats.

From 1897 to 1900 a round-robin series took place after the regular season. This series usually included all teams, so even the wooden spoon winner could still win the premiership.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

This format was changed after Melbourne won the 1900 premiership after finishing the regular season in sixth (out of eight teams).

The competition settled on a top-four finals structure in 1901, albeit with several strange variations over the following decades.

From 1901 to 1930, the minor premier was guaranteed to play in the grand final. If did not win it, they could challenge the winner to a second grand final.

This "right of challenge" format led to suspicion of minor premiers deliberately losing finals so they could earn more money from playing an extra final.

From 1931 to 1971, the Page-McIntyre system was implemented. This top-four system gave a double chance to the top two teams, but removed the controversial challenge rule for the minor premiers.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Since 1972, the number of finalists has grown from five to ten, as the number of teams in the competition has increased.

These different formats have all aimed to reward teams for a strong regular season, without giving the top teams an unfair advantage in the finals.

Many previous finals formats have initially received similar criticism about being a cash grab and rewarding mediocrity.

It might be here to stay

More finalists this year does mean more clubs and more fans being engaged for longer.

However, the closeness of the fight for the top ten and the quality of games in the wildcard round could be the most important factor for ensuring acceptance of this most recent finals change.

title: Short-stay units to ease pressure on crowded EDs
text:
A multi-million dollar plan will expand hospital short-stay units in a bid to reduce crowding in one state's bursting emergency departments.

The NSW government on Monday announced it would direct $130.7 million to building 22 treatment spaces this financial year.

The state's public hospitals have noted more than 500,000 emergency short-stay admissions since the beginning of 2024.

Hospitals treat and observe patients who require care past their initial emergency room assessment in short-stay units.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Campbelltown, Nepean, Maitland, John Hunter, St George and Wyong hospitals will receive the additional spaces.

A further eight spaces will be built over the 2027/28 financial year.

Health Services Union NSW Secretary Gerard Hayes welcomed the investment as absolutely essential to smooth functioning.

Patients treated in short-stay units often don't need to be admitted to a hospital ward. (Mick Tsikas/AAP PHOTOS)

"This investment is critical, as is a broader range of measures aimed at expanding scope of practice to empower more of the health workforce to use more of their skills so we can keep patients moving through the hospital system," he told AAP.

Premier Chris Minns said the additional units would alleviate stress from emergency departments under constant and sustained pressure, regardless of the time of the year.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"At hospitals which already have a short stay unit in the ED we're seeing patients with semi-urgent conditions treated and back home quicker without needing to be admitted to a traditional ward in most cases," he said.

Health Minister Ryan Park said short stay units helped enhance ED capacity, streamline patient flow, and improve patient experience.

Earlier in August, Mr Minns asked patients to avoid the emergency room after a record day of winter presentations.

Nearly 10,000 presentations to Sydney EDs the day prior marked the biggest recorded winter day, according to Mr Park.
